utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, please bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have Dr. Mujezinovic brought in, so that we can continue with the cross-examination, which will be carried out either by Mr. Nobilo or by Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I should like to remind you that you are still under oath and that now, Mr. Nobilo is going to continue his cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo, good morning. Please continue with your cross-examination. DR. MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours. Dr. Mujezinovic. Yesterday, we were speaking about the co-ordinating committee for the protection of Muslims so we shall try to reduce it to one or two questions. The members of that committee responsible for the police, were they Saban Mahmutovic and Djidic Sefkija in charge of national defence? Please tell me, if the co-ordinating committee were to conclude that certain decisions of the HVO government were to the detriment of the Muslims, what would those two members responsible for the police and national defence respectively and the decisions have to do with their two spheres of activity? Would they implement the decision of the government and write protest letters or would they implement decisions of the co-ordinating committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would always issue statements and if the head of the police who reported on daily events in Vitez and through the media -- we issued statements, as I said. At a meeting, and I spoke about that yesterday, we had decided that we would not accept a single nation government in Vitez, and we felt that this was an attack against the legal authorities in Vitez, and that the legality of all authorities had been violated, so the only means we resorted to was the issuance of statements which may be written by Mr. Djidic Sefkija or by Mr. Saban Mahmutovic, the two people you mentioned, and these would be signed by the co-ordinating committee for the protection of the interests of Muslims in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But did those two implement the decisions of the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not obliged to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the first parade of the Territorial Defence which later developed into the BH-Army in Vitez? Were you present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I came towards the end of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a rostrum, a stand, a place of honour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing in particular as far as I can remember, I came towards the end, it was already over. It was in the secondary school centre in Vitez, and Mr. Djidic Sefkija had reviewed the units, this was already over, I did not spend much time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Djidic Sefkija report to anyone on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said during the direct examination, and I cite: "I personally had a great many problems with armed Muslims and Croats performing my duties."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you explain what it is you meant? You explained to us the problems with the armed Croats. Can you explain to us what problems you had with armed Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yesterday that one of our tasks was to prevent any incidents in Vitez, to avoid all possible clashes. I shall give you just one example in Vitez. About November, two soldiers of the BH-Army were killed, one was wounded. After that, soldiers of the BH-Army captured six HVO soldiers, disarmed them and beat them up. I did not know about it; it happened at night. In the morning, I attended a meeting when Mr. Djidic Sefkija stated that the captured HVO soldiers had to be released, because Mr. Blaskic was threatening him. If they were not released he would set fire to his headquarters and to him. I went to the village of Kruscica where the HVO soldiers who had been captured were being held and I told them they had to be released. Unfortunately, some of them were badly beaten and I was told they had found a bag with gold jewellery on one of the soldiers, earrings, bracelets, rings, and on one of the earrings, they had found traces of blood. This soldier was called Dragan Botic. I was told then that he was terribly beaten by Behaija Kavazovic, a soldier of the BH-Army and he had also mistreated them. After this the soldiers were released. As far as I know, the BH-Army soldiers were arrested and taken to prison. I was threatened by other BH-Army soldiers and told, "Doctor, you are treating them, you are helping them and they are killing us." The Commander of that part of the BH-Army, Hakija Dzelilovic, said to me on a number of occasions, "People do not know what you are doing, they will shoot at you", but I was frequently in the company of HVO soldiers, particularly when we were refurbishing the Kruscica motel to make a war hospital there. There were threats made to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you listed a series of incidents committed by members of the HVO army against inhabitants of Vitez. Can you tell me, in general terms, without going into any details, that members of the BH-Army would provoke an incident and resort to violence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you quite frankly that there were occasionally tit for tats; for instance if HVO soldiers disarmed a BH soldier, then these would disarm HVO soldiers. There were this kind of incidents; or if they confiscated a car, for instance, then BH-Army soldiers would reciprocate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any incidents with the use of firearms on both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just told you a story when there were some killed and wounded people. I do not know what more I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from this isolated incident that you have described, was it a phenomenon that repeated itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that there was reciprocation. I do not know to what extent and how many, but we tried to deal with these problems and official statements were issued, telling them not to disarm one another, to allow convoys to pass through checkpoints, of course, after being announced in advance, not to mistreat people at checkpoints and not to rob them, but after that, there was reciprocation on the other side too, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned regarding the statement that you signed and the circumstances under which you signed it that there were some soldiers extraneous to the region. Do you know whether there were any units from Herzegovina in your municipality at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a unit came which was housed in the elementary school in Dubravica and on one occasion I visited an elderly sick Croat, Ivica Marijanovic. I think this was some time in January, the second half, I am not sure. The man complained that the soldiers were disturbing him. He went over to them and asked them, "Why are you shooting?" They answered, "We are shooting at the birds." When these people came to Vitez, it was really hell. I was not told anything officially, but I heard that they were a unit from somewhere. Where they came from I do not know, but I know they were not from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this Marijanovic, is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, that the intensity of these incidents increased when this unit arrived in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw these soldiers myself, I saw them breaking up a butcher's shop together with HVO units from Vitez, then the city pharmacy. I saw this myself, and I stated yesterday that this was after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this unit have any special patches on their sleeves to differentiate them from the local ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had a leaf, an oak leaf I think, or a elm leaf. They could be seen in the afternoons. I did not move around much because I did not dare. I moved in my car until it was taken away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You spoke about robberies at local checkpoints. Can you tell me whether these robberies had any ethnic characteristics or was everyone robbed, Muslims and Croats alike, anyone who had any valuables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local Muslims were indeed robbed, but so were Croats who were not from Vitez. They complained to me, people who were travelling with Muslims, for instance people who came from the region of Tesanj. On one occasion I appeared on local television in October. Some young men had been deprived of their vehicle, of their car and they asked me to help them. This was a mixed group; there were Muslims and Croats in it. They came to the infirmary and asked me to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know of any Croatian business that was blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that in the district of Rijeka, Nikica Gotovac's shop was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and Ivica Santic asked me whether I knew anything about the case. This is a suburb of Vitez actually. I heard from people from the area that an HVO soldier had threatened in the evening, demanding 10,000 marks from the owner of the establishment, and that is what I told Ivica Santic. He was a rather aggressive person; he did not behave quite normally. He was very aggressive with weapons, and I told him that people were saying that this young man had thrown a hand grenade into the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any other cases of establishments owned by Croats being blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was reported that in Stari Vitez, a shop had been looted owned by Nikola Krisanovic. I do not recall any other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the existence of criminal gangs wearing uniforms and engaging in crime proper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, a soldier is a soldier, and if he is a soldier he has his command to answer to. The command has to be responsible for uniformed soldiers and has to sanction them. At official meetings, Anto Valenta would frequently say, "It is an informal armed group that is responsible." However, in Vitez, HVO had a lot of troops that were very well armed and very well organised. As a person, I was surprised that an armed group could do such things when there was so many armed formations around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How can you distinguish a soldier from a civilian? By what? What is your way to distinguish them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers wear uniforms. In Vitez, the soldiers were wearing black and camouflage uniforms of the HVO, and the BH-Army soldiers mostly wore camouflage uniforms with the insignia of the BH-Army. Some of them wore black uniforms but very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In those days, in 1993, beginning of 1993, when you moved around Vitez, particularly in the areas where the Croats were in the majority, were the men mostly in uniform or were uniformed people in a minority? What was the ratio between civilians and uniformed people? Who were in the majority in the streets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation in Vitez in the morning appeared almost normal. I went to work normally and then in the afternoon and in the evenings, the situation deteriorated. There would be firing, grenades would go off. People mostly kept to their homes. In downtown Vitez, there were not places exclusively inhabited by Muslims and others by Croats, particularly in these apartment buildings. The tenants were ethnically mixed, one flat next to another, or even houses were mixed too in the area of Vitez under the control of the HVO, with the exception of the village of Rijeka for instance which was perhaps 90 per cent inhabited by Croats. As I was saying, in the mornings things were almost normal, but frequently, we would see the results of the previous night, that some establishments were destroyed, devastated, or looted, the windows having been broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I was asking you whether the men were predominantly in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the proportion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were far more troops, soldiers,.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So there were more men in uniform than in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember the period of October 1992 and the conflict that occurred in Novi Travnik and the roadblocks in Ahmici. You just mentioned that in passing. What was it that happened in Novi Travnik in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my testimony yesterday, I mentioned that I was the doctor on duty in the internal medicine ward in Travnik. This duty lasted 48 hours over the weekend, and on Monday when I was handing over my duty, the wounded started coming in from Novi Travnik. I learnt in the hospital already that there had been a conflict between the BH-Army and the HVO in Novi Travnik. I went to do some work in the clinic in Vitez, and went home to sleep. The next day, when I went to work, I wanted to take my car because I worked at several places and my neighbour, Nikola Omerdic, told me not to take my car because it would be taken away from me by HVO soldiers. I asked why and he said, "You see, there has been a conflict." "Where?" "In Ahmici", he said. I went to the health centre and there the staff were rather scared and as the acting doctor of the health centre, it is a big building with a lot of glass, and I said that we had to move to the reserve location that we had which was safer, so we moved. During the day we could hear fire later, but we admitted four or five Muslim civilians that day. My colleague Dr. Bruno Buzuk, a dentist, who was then acting as a kind of health minister in the HVO government, warned the personnel, the staff, not to go out into the street because Muslim snipers were shooting. I asked him, "Bruno, what do you mean? How come Muslim snipers when Muslim civilians are coming to the hospital wounded?" He gave me an uncertain answer, a vague answer. In the course of the day, we did not have too much work to do, and in the afternoon, a friend of mine, a Croat, came and told me that the BH-Army had confiscated his car. Ilija Safradin is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did any dead soldier from either side arrive from Ahmici on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you go to the roadblock in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just sent drivers because we were told there were some people wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned your colleague from Zenica in Nadioci who did an inquest of the dead body destroyed by an explosion. Do you know who the perpetrator of that act was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know, but I was called in as a doctor to establish death and my colleague who had only just come from Zenica, Pehar, I do not remember his first name, who would come to work with us from time to time, and ask him to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, you explained that yesterday. In the direct examination, you said that the municipal government of HVO gave you assurances in writing that the situation would calm down if you recognised the authority of that government. Have I remembered what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told orally that we the Muslims in Vitez must accept the new HVO government and that officials of Muslim nationality in that government from the civilian branch, the civil police, the defence, should take their posts in that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, you explained that, but if you had accepted that, would the situation have calmed down or would it have gone the way it did anyway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it was not up to me alone to decide, I was just one of the members of the SDA. The opinion of people was as follows, that the legitimacy of the legal authorities had been violated since the flags of the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian state had been hoisted, that this was an attack against the very state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, you already said that. Could you just tell me what you think, whether the situation would have calmed down or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what would have happened. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In that context, when the HVO wanted to subjugate you, do you know anything about the joint command for Central Bosnia between the BH-Army and the HVO, Prkacin, Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of both of them. Personally I am not acquainted with either. I was told they were co-operating well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned Ante Prkacin and Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard at meetings that they were co-operating quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you do not know the details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned Cerkez as the commander of the HVO already in 1992 in Vitez. What was Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak was elected after the elections as head of the MUP or SUP in Vitez, and that was his position throughout 1990 and the first half of 1991, until he became President of the HDZ for Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Pero Skopljak, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But I am asking about Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak, I do not know exactly, I think that he was involved with defence affairs. Stipo Krizanac was elected to that post at the formal elections, but he took over in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he superior to Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know the structure in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very briefly, please, you have identified on the photograph Prosecutor Anto Valenta, Ignjac Kostroman and Dario Kordic wearing military uniforms. Were they civilian or military officials as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Dario Kordic is concerned, he was always in military uniform. I never saw him in civilian clothes. We were just told that he was President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that he held the rank of colonel, so he performed both positions. He had military rank. I do not know exactly what his role was, but that is how he was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about Anto Valenta? Did he have any military role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Valenta was mostly in uniform and in the second half of 1992, he was also introduced as one of the Vice-Presidents of Herceg-Bosna. What exactly his position was in the hierarchy I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the medical centre and today in Kruscica as well, you told us you were preparing a war hospital. Did you have a surgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a small minor surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These are minor injuries, for instance of the stomach or the head. This was something that we were not equipped for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you did not have a proper surgical theatre, operation room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had no anaesthetics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After the beginning of the conflict, was your house guarded by the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, after 16th April 1993, was your house or rather your apartment guarded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see from my apartment and at my entrance to the apartment building I was living in, there were armed people, not policemen but mostly local people who were armed and we were prohibited from moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see this as protection or control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first morning, my immediate neighbour came to tell me that my family and I would be executed because we had not been obedient. My family and my neighbours were under terrible pressure and fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you feel safer with armed people in front of your apartment or not; that is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have preferred not to have anybody armed there, because I thought that we did not need armed people in town. That was the opinion I upheld in Vitez, only the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But when the war broke out, did you see this as providing greater security or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this as withholding freedom of movement, as a kind of arrest, not just for me but for all the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the fact that you were driven by car to your work and back? Was this to protect you or to limit your freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who made the decision, but I was driven to and from work all the time. Dragan Petrovic was my driver. He was also my neighbour; I knew him very well. He was polite towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So did you consider this as a service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was glad that somebody would talk to me normally. You see, as a doctor, we did a lot of hard work. I never thought about these things, I concentrated on saving as many lives as possible. MR.. HARMON: Excuse me, your Honour, I would ask that Mr. Nobilo allows the witness to conclude his answer before he asks the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I support what the Prosecutor has said. I think that some of these matters were reviewed in private session yesterday, I think, at the request of the Prosecution, some of the aspects of the questions you are putting to the witness now. I am just taking advantage of the opportunity to indicate this, but otherwise, please continue and bear this in mind. MR.. NOBILO: Mr. President, I absolutely have in mind the aspects of the private session. The thing with the driver, this was regular going to work and coming back from work. Perhaps I have been interrupting the witness a bit because I have been trying to speed things up. Thank you. Dr. Mujezinovic, let us sum this up. Your political work in the municipality of Vitez, when did it begin, what month, and when did it end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My political work began in September 1991, and finished on 1st November 1995. Since then, I have not been involved in any political or whatever things. I have been working as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in Vitez -- I imagine that you stopped working politically when you left Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was always on the territory of the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, if we confine ourselves to the beginning of your political work in the municipality of Vitez, until the day you left your apartment or perhaps until the outbreak of the war, so April 16th, how many meetings did you have with the representatives of the Croatian people as you tried to quiet things down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Approximately, per month or per week, if you can give me a figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that I did not take part in all these meetings, because I had three places where I worked. At least twice a week, perhaps even more often, but I did not participate in all meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition, you said that there were private contacts -- please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, the co-ordinating committee for protecting the interests of Muslims in Vitez, it was said that Fuad Kaknjo and Kajmovic Munir as the President of the SDA in Vitez, that they should permanently, every day, be in touch with Ivan Santic and co-operate with him and Anto Valenta and Pero Skopljak, to be in touch every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we say that in that period there were private contacts and official contacts, that there were several hundred such contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Private, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And official.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell exactly. You see, try to understand me, I could not go from the place where I worked to my home without meeting, say, five different people who would stop me and that is about 500 metres; that is only when I went home. Whether it was 100, 200, 500 or 1,000 I really cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you say in all fairness that as a citizen, as a politician, if that is the proper word to use, that you did everything that you could, that you talked to everyone, to all people who were important, in order to resolve the situation in Vitez? Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I am a doctor, and a citizen, and then a politician. I should say to you that absolutely, truly absolutely, I exposed myself to danger. I could have lost my life on many occasions, but I did this so that I could do everything in my ability to prevent these things in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. How many times did you talk to Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially I never met Mr. Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know him here? Can you recognise him here now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the gentleman from television and from the street, but officially, I never met him, nor did I ever talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see an order issued by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a meeting some time in October, it was showed to us -- there was a document showing that we were being supported by Commander Tihofil Blaskic, commander of operations for central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you mean by support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to say through his orders he would prohibit looting, robbery at checkpoints, that he would make every effort to stop the torching of houses of prominent Muslims; that is what we were told at an official meeting, and personally, if you want me to use the Croat word, the other word for personally, we never talked on the phone. I only saw him in Vitez, I mean I first saw him with the HVO army when the army was being sworn in and a soldier had fainted there, so I was there. That was the first time I physically saw his face. I do not know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You do not know anything else about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. MR.. NOBILO: Mr. President, I have completed my questioning and my colleague Mr. Hayman will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, learned colleagues, Dr. Mujezinovic. If at any time in my questioning you would be more comfortable responding to a question excluding the public, that is in closed session, please so indicate. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps as I am asking my first questions, your Honour, the Registrar could retrieve exhibit 45; that will be the first exhibit I will be using. Turning to the subject of the photograph you were shown of Messrs Valenta, Kordic and, I believe, Skopljak, all in uniform, and about which you had a recent exchange with my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, you said, I believe, that on the occasion you met Mr. Kordic, he was introduced to you as a colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said in your earlier testimony that you met Mr. Kordic on one occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in my statement that on several occasions I was officially present at meetings at the level of the Travnik region or Busovaca Novi Travnik region, Travnik region where Dario Kordic was present too. On one occasion, I was in charge of organising the health services in Vitez, organising health services in a war situation with Dr. Bruno Buzuk. I went to Busovaca because he had suggested it to me because we needed quite a few things in order to get things going, and he told me that the only person who could help was -- we went to the hotel Tisa and he told me that Dario Kordic was a Colonel. I did not know that his mother was a doctor. I did not know then that he went to school in Vitez, I mean that he went to high school in Vitez. He asked me, "What is up, doctor?" I told him why I came and he took a paper, he signed it and he said, "Take this paper, go to Grude and bring in three War Hospitals." After that, privately, I had no contacts with Dario Kordic, except at official meetings, and I heard him on radio and television and at official meetings where we were among the people who were attending them.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Most of my questions will call for a yes or no answer. If you wish to elaborate, you may, but I would ask that you attempt to limit your answer to the question and not volunteer additional information. I am sure after my examination if you feel that I have not given you full opportunity to explain your answers, the Prosecutor will in his redirect. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be permitted to answer questions fully and completely and in the way he is comfortable in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: His answers have to be responsive, your Honour, and we are having difficulty in that regard, with all due respect to counsel and to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, let us not dispute, have a quarrel on answers that have still not been given. Mr. Hayman, you put the questions; the Prosecutor will see whether he wants to object to them and above all, the judges. You may have a preference regarding the answer, that it should be brief, but the witness is free to answer those questions as he wishes. Mr. Hayman, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked you if you were ever introduced to Mr. Kordic. Can you answer that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, was he introduced to you as a colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Bruno Buzuk, as I just told you; I just told you the story now -- I do not know why I should be repeating this -- in the hotel Tisa, Dr. Bruno Buzuk introduced Dario Kordic to me as a colonel. It was very early and I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what Tihomir Blaskic's rank was in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. I think he is a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel. I do not know the ranks in the HVO. I think he is a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel. I do not know, I really do not know their hierarchy. I think he is something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the relationship in the HVO military chain of command between Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure; I can only give you my opinion. Is that what you wish?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you can tell us anything I am inviting you to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, a far higher post was held by Dario Kordic, political and military, and I do not know whose post in the military hierarchy of the HVO was higher; who was subordinated to whom, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt that Dario Kordic held such a high position that he was in a position to give direct orders to HVO troops; do you have any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could directly issue such orders, I do not know really to what extent. I can claim that I am not familiar with the military hierarchy in the army of the HVO. I do not know. I am not familiar with these military affairs and this military hierarchy in the HVO. I truly do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you do not know the answer to a question, please tell us that you do not know. We have placed on the easel Prosecutor exhibit 45, on top of which has been placed a plastic overlay. What I am going to ask is -- first I will mark the overlay so that it can be placed again in the same location for accuracy. Then I am going to ask that you mark certain borders. First, if I may take a moment, your Honour, I would like to mark the transparency so that its position can be replicated. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have not posed a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. Doctor, I have now marked the transparency at the top on the right-hand side and around the legend box in red. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were a resident of Vitez in the 1980s and the early 1990s; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You know the neighbourhoods in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there a neighbourhood known as Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to, first let me ask you, to mark the boundaries of the neighbourhood known as Kolonija as you understand them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can respond to that. In Vitez, we called apartment buildings Kolonija, where there were several apartments, and we did not call family homes Kolonija. Only apartment buildings, we only called apartment buildings Kolonija and private family homes were never called Kolonija. For example in Stari Vitez and around that area, that was never called Kolonija, only apartment buildings. Do you really want me to draw that?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a general portion of Vitez stretching from somewhere to the east of the stadium to the east that was principally dominated by a number of good-sized or large apartment buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question or would you rather show us? Before you mark the easel, doctor, could you tell us what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apartment buildings in Vitez that we in Vitez called Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before you mark the easel, let me ask you, was there a neighbourhood known as Kolonija? If you could answer that question before you mark the transparency?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic did not have his earphones on when you asked that last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, before you mark the easel, can you tell us what you propose to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, are you afraid that there may be a difference between your question and what he is going to draw? You must choose. Either you are going to ask the witness to show you on the map what you consider to be the Kolonija and he will do it or not, or you ask him to answer a question regarding the Kolonija neighbourhood. If you ask him to mark on the map the Kolonija district, let him do it. If he makes a mistake, you will redo the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I want him to do that, your Honour. Let me ask you this question before you mark it. Can you mark a district or a neighbourhood that was known as Kolonija? Can you do that for us? Before you mark, can you answer my question, please? Would you please speak into the microphone by the easel so the interpreters can pick up what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you. What do you really want? Do you want me to draw the Kolonija neighbourhood? Do you want me to encircle it with a red pen? What is the neighbourhood of Vitez what was called Kolonija; is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us try and make a little progress after all. Listen, I think you asked the witness to indicate on the map the Kolonija neighbourhood. Dr. Mujezinovic, can you please show us on the map what you consider to be the Kolonija neighbourhood and then we will go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local community of Kolonija, this part of Vitez (drawing) this way, this way too. That would be Kolonija approximately, a residential area with big apartment buildings. This was a local community. This was also the local community, you know, but we specifically called this neighbourhood, these big apartment buildings, Kolonija, with the municipal administrative centre; and the local community, I do not know what are all the places that belong to the local community itself. This is Gradina; probably that belonged to it. Kruscica is up here.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, let me join you for a moment and make sure that the boundaries have been clearly marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, that is Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Am I accurately tracing over your line, doctor, to make it appear more clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did you ask me about the local community of Kolonija or did you ask me about the neighbourhood of Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked you about the neighbourhood. Is that what you marked on the map in red?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that different from the local community of Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the local community of Kolonija insofar as it is different from the neighbourhood Kolonija. Without marking it, can you describe it in words? Is it larger or smaller?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is bigger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the local community is bigger and what you have marked is the smaller of the two, the neighbourhood Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see where I have traced over your line on the right-hand side of the transparency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have I accurately written over the line that you drew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to continue and if you would watch me, because I will ask you the same question when I have completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not there. The apartment buildings here, that is what we called Kolonija. Apartment buildings in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have I accurately traced over your line to mark it more clearly on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we called Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you; you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know officially, but we, the ordinary people, that is what we called Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present at a meeting in October 1992 concerning the roadblock that was established on the road from Busovaca to Vitez in the neighbourhood of Ahmici at which Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Santic came and met with a number of representatives of the civilian and military Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a doctor, I organised that meeting through Mr. Ivica Santic, and I think that Anders Levison was the name of the head of the UNHCR. I went to Stari Vitez to give a car back to a Croat. I went to the command of the TO in the high school and I was told there was some shooting the previous night, that the office of the commander of the TO had been hit, and that he was not there in the building but that he was at the reserve command position in Stari Vitez. I took an ambulance there. I was driven there by Stipo Kristo, the driver of the ambulance, a Croat, and I found Sefkija Djidic there, and I said why I came, that Ilija Safradin asked me to have his private car, an Opal Kadet, returned and he ordered Atilic Minet, his military policeman, to give me the keys to the Kadet back. He told me then that he received oral orders over the phone from Dzemo Merdan from Zenica -- I think then he was commander of the district staff in Zenica -- that roadblocks should be put in the village of Ahmici. He told me that the army on the front was changing and that he had very few forces in Ahmici and he asked me to get in touch with Ivan Santic or someone. Since I was on the friendliest terms out of all of them with Ivan Santic, I promised I would do whatever I could. I called Ivan Santic when I came back and I asked him -- I told him what Sefkija Djidic was asking for, and I said that he had asked for another meeting to be held the next day, or -- I do not know, I cannot remember. The next day the meeting was held. I went to that meeting, but as we were entering the premises, we first went to the office of Mr. Anders Levison and then to the post office. I came back because, from the direction of Gradina, what I had just been drawing, a lot of shooting could be heard and I did not know what it was all about. I said that I could not be present at a place where there was shooting. I went back about -- I was about 100 metres away from the post office, so I did not attend that meeting but I attended the meeting the next day in the office of Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At any point in October 1992, were you told why Ahmici was chosen as the location for this roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that there was a conflict between the BH-Army and the HVO in Travnik, and that units from Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo, were moving on to Novi Travnik; they were receiving orders to stop them. Sefkija Djidic told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about why Ahmici was chosen as the location for the roadblock to stop HVO troops going to Travnik or Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Ahmici is just on the main road, the main communications line and that is somewhere nearby, the boundary between Vitez and Busovaca municipalities. I was not told anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you attend one meeting at which also Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Santic appeared concerning this issue of the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I attended the first meeting -- not the first meeting, but I did attend the second meeting where several conclusions were adopted and one of the conclusions was to go on local television to have the situation calmed down and to present the conclusions from that meeting. I went on local television, together with Pero Skopljak and the local priest and the local Haji, the Muslim priest.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know: at the time of this meeting was the roadblock still in place or had it been cleared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I scheduled and organised meetings, I think that Dr. Bruno Buzuk -- he told us, because we heard that there were wounded, that the army that had set out had already passed by, and they told us that there were wounded in Ahmici, and we sent an ambulance three times that was driven by Dusko Bulajic; we sent it to Ahmici to bring in the wounded. He brought in a man called Kajmakovic Nasib, 55 years old in civilian clothes, and I had gone to have lunch when that happened. I told you about that already. I found him lying there and an HVO soldier had hit him, and it is only thanks to Dr. Bruno and the medical staff that we put him into the ambulance and we sent him to an orthopaedic surgeon in Zenica because his shoulder was shattered, I think. I was called by Munir Kajmovic the head of the SDA party to appear on local television but otherwise he appeared on local television to explain to the people in Vitez the political situation. I was only his deputy, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the purpose of you and the other three individuals going on television was to calm the situation in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you present at any meeting where Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Santic came and appealed to representatives of the Muslim civilian and military authorities to remove the roadblock from Ahmici so that a greater conflict would not occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already told you that at that time, I was the doctor on duty at the general hospital in Travnik, in the ward for internal medicine, and I did not attend that meeting, but when I came to work, they told me in the health centre that on the initiative of Franjo Tibold, Mario Cerkez and Djidic Sefkija had come to the health centre in Vitez and that they did not agree on anything and that war was going to happen. That is what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were not told then, I take it, that at that meeting there was a request by Cerkez --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present at any official meeting. I apologise. Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You said you were told certain things about this earlier meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the medical personnel who were working there in the health clinic, they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether or not Mr. Cerkez and/or Mr. Santic made a request at this earlier meeting that the roadblock in Ahmici be removed in order to avoid a greater conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were people working in the health centre, nurses, doctors, they probably did not know anything about this. They just told me that Djidic Sefkija and Mario Cerkez had been to the health centre. That is what they told me at that time, and then I heard from others that there had been previous meetings, but I did not attend that meeting, because I was the doctor on duty in the Travnik hospital. I was on duty for the weekend and I was working in the health centre, so I knew nothing about the meeting, I was very tired, I went home to sleep. I think that meeting took place in the afternoon of the 19th, but I did not know about it, otherwise I would have attended.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from any source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I think perhaps we can have a break, except if the Prosecutor has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question has been asked and answered a number of times. The witness has given his answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He has said he was not there, he was told certain things by the medical staff but he has also said he was told something later by other people. I respectfully suggest to my friend and colleague that I am navigating this path and I am almost done but I am trying to navigate through it. I am not asking the same question over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Listen, the Trial Chamber thanks you and invites you to a 20-minute break until 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, how much time have you planned for your cross-examination, approximately of course?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will certainly finish by 1.00, your Honour, and if we can keep the exchanges shorter rather than longer I hope to be done in 40 or 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you: in October 1992, did you see any wounded HVO as a result of the conflict in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not getting an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you resume, please? Repeat what you said, doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said that when I was leaving the hospital compound in Travnik I was told that the wounded were being admitted to surgery. I did not look to see whether they were members of the BH-Army or HVO soldiers. I really did not look because I had to go back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you did not see any wounded on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them being brought in in ambulances to the surgery. People were being carried out to the surgical centre, the wounded. I did not pay any attention to see who they were. I had to go back to Vitez, because I did not work in the surgical department but at the internal medicine department.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were these individuals coming out of ambulances or other vehicles dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left the hospital in my car, I asked what was happening: the wounded were being brought in to the hospital. I told you that I did not pay attention at all, because it was not my responsibility as a doctor. It was just the medical staff who told me that these were the wounded from Novi Travnik and there were several ambulances in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you said you saw them coming in to the hospital. Do you recall whether or not they were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were being brought in, driven in, I said. I told you that I saw the ambulances driving in the wounded from Novi Travnik. I did not describe who I saw, I just asked what was happening, and the medical staff told me that they were the wounded from Novi Travnik, and that there had been a conflict in Novi Travnik. In my statement, I did not say whether they were civilians or soldiers, whether they belonged to the HVO or the BH-Army. I did not say that; I just learned because of these many ambulances and private vehicles arriving. It was difficult for me to drive out, there was such a crowd. That is how I learnt what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you saw no wounded on that occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the ambulances; that is what I said, and people in the ambulances. I did not pay attention, I just asked what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During the April 1993 conflict, did you see wounded soldiers while performing work at a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what month?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: April 1993 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I see wounded soldiers? Yes, wounded soldiers, HVO soldiers did come, wounded soldiers of the BH-Army did not come. There were civilians, Bosniaks there were wounded who did come. No soldier of the BH-Army, at least not anyone wearing a uniform, came to see me. There were people who were wounded who, by their age and medical condition could have been soldiers, but they were not wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On what day or days did you see wounded HVO soldiers in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th April, I told you that a military policeman of the HVO, Dragan Calic, brought me from my apartment to work in the medical centre, the one that had been adjusted to wartime conditions. I worked very hard that day. I admitted a large number of HVO soldiers with various kinds of injuries, from light ones to very grave ones. In the course of my working hours, one dead soldier was brought in from the area of Gacice, the village of Gacice, near Vitez. I knew him personally; he was a goalkeeper in a village football club in the village of Jardol, so we were admitted. The wounded, there were many; I do not know how many. There is a record, a medical record there, and this can be checked, both the diagnoses and where people were transferred to and these records were left in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you estimate the number of wounded soldiers you saw at the medical facility on April 19th 1993 in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what to say, but there were many. I worked all day, I did not even put down everything in the book, I was just saying what people should be given as medication, whether they should be sent to Travnik, Zenica or Split, because I was very familiar with the capacities of all the various hospitals in our part of Bosnia; for instance a man with a head injury could not be sent to Travnik because we did not have the appropriate surgeons. I would have to have them transferred to Zenica or Split. There were many; I worked all day, not just me but all of us were working.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you estimate? Were there more than 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were there more than 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. So as not to make up any figures, please check with the medical protocol or records; each one is registered there. I could say 1,000, 5,000, I really do not know, but there are medical records and every single injury has been entered, and even if a death occurred it has been entered. All I know is that I worked very hard, that I was very tired and so were all the staff members.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you estimate what percentage of the wounded HVO soldiers you saw on April 19th 1993 were from the Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot; I did not pay attention. In the medical profession our main concern is the actual condition of the patient, to provide life-saving treatment, to stop haemorrhaging, to apply a catheter, a tube to provide general medical treatment and aid, so that I paid very little attention to other things. I may see that a man was in an uniform or in civilian clothes, but I really could not tell what kind of uniform they were wearing and I think this applies to all the staff because that was not important to us. What was important to us was to save the person's life, so I did not pay any attention to that, nor did the others. There was a great deal to do; we did not have time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your testimony you are unable to say whether you treated any soldiers from the Vitezovi unit on April 19th 1993; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, the question has been asked and answered. He said he did not pay attention; his main effort was to treat and save the lives of the people who came into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please change your question, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked the usher to provide the witness with a prior statement that he gave in regard to this matter, and I have copies attached, your Honour, for the court, the Prosecutor's office and the Registrar. (Handed). Doctor, this statement is in English. Let me ask you initially to turn to the last page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Counsel, can you wait until we get a copy of it before you start questioning? (Handed). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, could you turn to the last page of the statement? Do you see the last page? Have you found the last page of the statement, doctor? I am not asking you to read it; I am asking you if you have found the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the last page, but it is of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is correct. Do you recognise your signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was this statement read to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This statement, when I signed it, there was a version in the Bosnian language, and I said that the translation was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a written version in the Bosnian language that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, we have not been provided with that copy of the witness's statement and I would lodge that formal request with the Office of the Prosecutor and with the court. Doctor, was this statement read to you or did you read a written Bosnian version of this statement before you signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, what are you asking from the Registry and the Tribunal? What exactly are you asking? Mr. Registrar, will you please take note of the request. It is a statement that was translated into English on the basis of a statement made by Mr. Mujezinovic on 3rd February 1997. What is it that you do not have?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am making a formal record, your Honour, that we have been told in the past that no written Bosnian statements were prepared, that all statements were prepared in English and were translated for the witness. This witness has stated that he saw and read a written statement containing apparently, substantially at least, the content of this statement in the Bosnian language. That is the statement we have never been provided with if in fact it existed and rather than write a letter to the Prosecutor's Office, I wish to put in the record we have not been provided with that statement. If it exists, I believe it is due to us under the Rules. I do not wish to hold up the hearing; I am not asking to resolve that issue now. I am just making a note of it and I wish to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record I do not know of the existence of a Bosnian statement, a translation of this particular statement. I will make an enquiry over the next recess and if one is available I will provide it to counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before having an enquiry, perhaps we can ask Mr. Kehoe, because he took this statement, if I understood well, to speed up the proceedings. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not get a translation in English of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was saying that before we make any enquiries, Mr. Kehoe took this statement. Perhaps he can give us some clarification which would speed up the debate. Mr. Kehoe? Except, if you prefer, Mr. Kehoe to make the enquiry later? I do not want to substitute the enquiry work of the Prosecutor. Mr. Kehoe, do you remember when the statement was taken, I assume it was taken in Serbo-Croatian or in Bosnian to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. The statement was taken and I was present during the questioning by Mr. Bajawa who is an investigator here. To my knowledge, there was never any Bosnian statement or translation of this particular document. There was a prior statement that was taken, I am not sure if it is referred to here. The prefatory language says: "I, Muhamed Mujezinovic, understand this is by way of addendum to my earlier statement and with the intention to clarify certain points arising from my earlier statement." That is the prefatory language. With regard to any translation of the earlier statement, Mr. President, I simply do not know. I was present during this; this was typed, and signed by Mr. Mujezinovic. I was not present with regard to the earlier statement. I do not know whether or not there was any translation to that, and that is the enquiry that Mr. Harmon said will be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment, please. Mr. Mujezinovic, you certainly recognise this statement because you signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So there was an interpreter who retranslated it back into your language before you signed it? Surely you did not sign the English version which is not your mother-tongue. Are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I signed a previous statement in the Bosnian language. I signed it because I did not have time and I said that it was a very poor version. This statement was translated to me orally, this other one that I signed, this one. This one was not in Bosnian, but the previous statement that I made and to which I objected regarding the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand, doctor. I am not talking about the previous statement, I am talking about this statement. It has been signed by you and you recognise the signature. It is in English. When you signed it, was there someone to read it to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And it was then that you said that the translation was poor. I think we close the incident for the moment. We give the floor again to Mr. Hayman and you will have an opportunity to clarify your thoughts through the cross-examination by Mr. Hayman. I consider the incident closed. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If the usher could assist the witness in placing the page marked 3 in the upper right-hand corner of this document and assist in focusing the ELMO on the next to last paragraph of that page, the page that begins, "During the April conflict ..." Doctor, I am going to read two or three sentences from this paragraph, and then the translators can translate those sentences into the various languages of the Tribunal, and then I am going to ask you about those sentences. Page 3 is the page that we need, not page 4, please. In the upper right-hand corner there are page numbers. The paragraph that I wish on the ELMO in some enlarged fashion is the next to last paragraph beginning, "During the April conflict ..." The page will need to be moved up on the ELMO, your Honour, for that paragraph to come into view. Further up, please. If now the image could be enlarged, please? Thank you. I will read two or three sentences from this paragraph, doctor: "During the April conflict, the Jokeri soldier, Vitezovi soldiers and other HVO soldiers that were wounded during the conflict were brought to the hospital." Skipping two sentences: "I would hear Croat staff of the hospital saying that here were Anto Furundzija soldiers, the Jokeri, or here are the Vitezovi soldiers. Most of the Vitezovi and Jokeri soldiers would have their faces painted. They would be wearing camouflage or black uniforms and would have knives hanging from their belts or tucked in their boots, along with pistols and other weapons." End of paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, but you asked me specifically about the wounded and not about who in all came to the War Hospital, who generally came to the War Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the portions I read, those are your statements and that is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my statement. I did say that, but in your previous question, you asked me specifically which were the wounded that we admitted, and I answered that in the case of the wounded, we did not pay attention, and in this statement, I said what is written here, and Anto Furundzija was one of the commanders, I think of the Jokeri and he came to me and he told me to go out and he asked me to give him my car keys. I told him that the car had been stolen from me and that he could check with the military and civilian police of the HVO that I had reported it. He told me, "Doctor, I know where your garage is. If I find your car in your garage, I will come back here and kill you." They would come. We had a department with beds for people to spend some time in.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I do not think there is any question pending. If you wish to further elaborate during redirect examination I have no opposition to that, but I do not think there is any question pending and I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object and I would like the witness to be permitted to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us please have the translation of Mr. Hayman's comment first. You have no further questions on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I have no question pending of the witness and he is giving a narrative which I respect his right to do but not during my examination when I have not posed a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to know, Mr. Prosecutor, what your objection is. It was not translated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My objection is, your Honour, the witness had not completed his answer. He was talking about "they were coming" and Mr. Hayman cut him off. My request is that Dr. Mujezinovic be permitted to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Doctor, please complete your answer as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence counsel asked me which wounded I had admitted to hospital. I answered that we did not pay attention to the uniforms. We simply looked at the wounds in order to save people's lives, and in my statement I said that people came to visit the wounded patients and the medical staff. The nurses would say, "These are Furundzija's soldiers; these are Kraljevic's", but not as visitors; they came under arms. I think I have made myself clear. If necessary please ask any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you please, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me reread the first paragraph of this sentence to you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have not finished with regard to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, and there will be other statements I suspect in this document that will be referred to before I am completed. To reread the first sentence of this paragraph, I would like you to listen carefully to it and tell us whether this is or is not your testimony. I quote: "During the April conflict, the Jokeri soldiers, Vitezovi soldiers and other HVO soldiers that were wounded during the conflict were brought to the hospital." Is that your testimony or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that all the wounded of the HVO had been brought in. I said there were no BH-Army soldiers, but among the HVO there were the Jokeri, the Vitezovi and, to be quite frank, for me they were all HVO, they just had different names.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it the sentence that I read is your testimony, that it is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that all the wounded soldiers were brought in from the HVO, and for me all these formations belonged to the HVO, the Jokeri and the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is the statement I read accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In Vitez in early 1993, were there armed gangs terrorising the entire population of Vitez at night?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, I would object. The question has been asked and answered before. Mr. Nobilo posed that question to the witness. If we are going to revisit the same areas that Mr. Nobilo has questioned, we are going to prolong these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The length of the debate does not depend exclusively on the will of the President and the judges. For the moment, I do not think that one can say that this question was put in the exact same words by Mr. Hayman. I am not sure; I do remember that questions regarding armed bands were put to the witness, so please let Mr. Hayman put his questions to the witness, and please continue, Mr. Hayman, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, would you agree with the statement that in early 1993, armed gangs were harrassing the people of Vitez and robbing them during the late night hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Marijan Skopljak form his own private unit of soldiers at any relevant time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was private, but it was said that Marijan Skopljak was the head of that group of some 30 people, but I think it was not a private group. Marijan Skopljak was the Minister of Defence in the second half of 1992, so whether it was private ... I think nothing in Vitez was private, with the exception of a few establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Marijan Skopljak take his own initiative to form a specific unit of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, your Honour? While we are distributing another document, what was this unit called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak's unit? They said in Vitez, among the people, this was the story, that Marijan Skopljak had a group of men, popularly known as the SS troops. I did not see any official paper saying that there was such a unit, nor did I see any other paper of that kind, but the people called this unit the SS unit.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they refer to it as Marijan Skopljak's unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am saying again, that was the story going around among the people, that their leader was Marijan Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you would look at this document that has just been provided to you -- it is also in English -- could you look at the last page please and see if you recognise your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is this a statement that you gave to the staff of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This statement I made to the investigating officer of The Hague Tribunal. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask the usher to assist and place the first page of the statement on the ELMO, focused on the portion of the bottom of the first page, about ten lines up from the bottom, that should be highlighted in yellow, and I would like to read a phrase to you and ask you if that is your testimony. That is fine, thank you from the technical box. The portion of this paragraph I would like to read reads as follows: "Skopljak Marijan formed a 30-man unit popularly called the 'SS' as in the Second World War and after this another unit was formed by Furundzija Anto called the Jokeri." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Anto Furundzija was in the TO until September and this unit was formed after September 1992, and the unit of Marijan Skopljak that was popularly known under this name started operating much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Darko Kraljevic also command his own unit of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stated that Darko Kraljevic -- in Bosnia there were party armies so the Croatian Party of Rights had its military unit in Vitez under the command of Darko Kraljevic, the so-called HOS. I have also previously said that this unit was disbanded some time in June or July and that it placed itself under the command of the HVO because Darko Kraljevic himself told me that while I was treating him. For a time he was dismissed and he had a psychological crisis and then the unit was changed -- changed its name to Vitezovi from HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that June or July of 1993, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was some time in June, I am not quite sure -- June.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of 1993, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, I am sorry, 1992. He himself, Darko Kraljevic, told me, as I have already said, that he had this crisis, that I went to treat him, that he was not involved for about a month and then afterwards, the unit was no longer called HOS but it was called Vitezovi. Some of them retained the HOS patch but officially they were known as Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak, was he from the local area in Vitez? Had he grown up there or lived there for a significant period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak was born in Vitez. He worked in the SPS factory, the Slobodan Princip Selo factory. We went together to elementary school; we know each other very well, I know his whole family; his uncle is Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Anto Furundzija, was he from the local area as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Anto Furundzija as a member of the military police in the TO. I was told that he was a former soldier. I never knew him before.
