utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And Darko Kraljevic; was the Kraljevic family resident in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kraljevics originally come from Herzegovina. It is called Siroko Brijeg now; before it was called Listica, but for many years three brothers lived in Vitez. The oldest one is Stanko Kraljevic and Darko is his son. I knew them very well. I also knew the Granic family, where his, Stanko's, wife came from. I know them well. Darko Kraljevic was born in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tihomir Blaskic did not grow up in the Vitez municipality to your knowledge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already told you, I did not meet Mr. Tihomir Blaskic formally. We do not have such surnames in Vitez. I just saw him on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During the period of the war you saw him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I never met him, I only saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described this conversation a moment ago with Darko Kraljevic in which he said that HOS had been disbanded. Do you have that subject matter in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What is the best date that you can put on that conversation, your most accurate date of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the first half of June, I think it was then. I cannot be quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of 1992; that is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In connection with the longer of the two statements that are before you, the one marked Defence exhibit 31 which is approximately 10 single-spaced pages, how long did that interview last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which one? I cannot remember -- I mean the first statement I made to The Hague investigators -- I really do not remember; it was very difficult. The interpreter during this first time was very poor; perhaps it went on for a couple of hours or even longer. I do not know, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it more than one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five or six hours; the interpreter was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then on another day, were you read the written statement which is exhibit D31 and asked whether it was true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was dissatisfied with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you signed it; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember if I signed it. Perhaps I did. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the last page of exhibit D31, can you tell us whether you recognise your signature above the date "Sunday, 16th July 1995", in the lower right-hand corner of the page marked 10 which is the last page of D31. That is the longer of the two statements, doctor. It may be on the ELMO, which is the overhead projector to your right. If you turn to the last page of that statement, the longer of the two statements. Did you indeed sign this statement, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In this statement, did you tell the investigators from the Tribunal of this conversation you have testified about today and yesterday in which Darko Kraljevic stated that his unit was disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember; I think I did not. I think I did not. I cannot remember; perhaps I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did the investigators ask you to relate your knowledge of the organisation and structure of the HVO and all units related to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked about the military formations that were operating in Vitez. I said that in the second half of 1992, the HVO operated only, that the units which had existed and had special names had simply chosen these names for themselves, but they were all under HVO command.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you told the investigators in your July 1995 interview that the HOS unit had been brought under HVO command by the second half of 1992; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know then, I have not got this here. I was asked as far as I can remember what were the units that were operated. I do not think they asked me when the HOS stopped operating. I know that I was asked what the HOS was like before: did they harass the Muslims before they became Vitezovi? I remember I was asked that. I said the local Muslims in Vitez were not harassed before by the Vitezovi in the first half of 1992. That is what they asked me and that is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you asked what the relationship of HOS was to the HVO? Do you recall whether the investigators in either interview asked you that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I have answered that question. I think I have answered that question. I do not know what you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am asking you to try and recall: in those interviews, in either interview, did the investigators ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has attempted to answer it. He has tried a number of times. I do not think there is any reason to continue asking the same question to this witness. The interview Mr. Hayman is referring to is dated 1995; it occurred over two years ago. The witness has said he does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is, your Honour, and there is no mention of this conversation in either written statement. I think it is important we determine how that came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, I think we have to introduce some reason into this debate. I will let you continue gladly, but I think we are turning round in a circle a little. This statement was made many months ago. The judges and I will decide whether we will admit it as evidence. I simply wish to draw your attention, Mr. Hayman, to the following: I do not think that you can instruct the Prosecutor. They did his work as best they could; you are free to ask all the questions you wish. You will be given the answers. You can use the contradictions, if any, in the statements, but I think that we must go ahead, so I ask you now to conclude on this point and to proceed to your next question. If not, I think the Tribunal, and I say this very seriously, will have to envisage limiting the time for interventions. We will ask that of the Prosecutor as well as of the Defence in that case, but do not forget the essential. Your strategy is yours, that of the Prosecution is theirs, but let us try and go forward. If you find that the witness is contradicting himself or not, it is up to you to use that, but please if you can speed up the proceedings and continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am trying, your Honour. I am trying very very hard to speed the proceedings up, I think the record will reflect how short my enquiries are and what kinds of answers they call for. Doctor, this conversation you have related with Darko Kraljevic concerning the disbanding of HOS, have you told it to any Tribunal investigator, talked about it or discussed it with any Tribunal investigator, prior to giving your testimony here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned to the Tribunal investigators that I had treated Darko Kraljevic medically. What else I told them ... I also think -- no, I do not think. I told them what Darko Kraljevic had told me and I said in my statement that for ten days, Darko Kraljevic kept coming in front of my apartment building -- his soldiers would come and pick me up at my apartment, they would bring me down to the car and then we would go to the health centre where he would receive his injection and then he would keep me in his car for two or three hours in order to talk to me. He talked to me about all sorts of things, I said that. Darko Kraljevic, among other things, said that the HVO, especially Skopljak Pero and Anto Valenta are talking him into destroying Muslim establishments. That is what I had said, and I do not know, I really do not see what you want. I do not know. I am absolutely clear. I told the investigators of The Hague Tribunal about this. They asked me who Darko Kraljevic was, I said he was from Vitez, his father was from Herzegovina, that it was a big family, three brothers lived in Vitez, that it was a young man whom I have known from his early childhood, that I knew his father, his father was head of the football club in Vitez and I was his deputy, I know his mother, his grandfather. I do not know what you want from me, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question, doctor, was: did you tell the investigators about this particular conversation? If you would answer that question I will leave this area and move on. The conversation in which you state Kraljevic had told you HOS had been disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Darko Kraljevic had told me that he had been replaced. Darko Kraljevic told me that he had been replaced, not that HOS had been disbanded. I do not know if I said that to the investigators. He told me that he had been replaced, and that he had handed over his duties to another person, I do not know who this other person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the President is going to intervene now. Doctor, Mr. Hayman has asked you a precise question. You will say yes or no. Did you speak about this to the investigators? Please answer with yes or no and we will go on to the next question. We cannot keep on going round in circles. I ask this in the interests of the proceedings. Please, Mr. Hayman, repeat the question for the last time. You can say, "I do not know"; "I do not wish to answer"; "yes it is true"; "no, it is not". The Trial Chamber is listening to your answer. Please put this question for the last time, very clearly and very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell the Tribunal investigators in either of your two interviews about the conversation you had with Kraljevic in which he said that HOS had been brought under the command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Doctor, please give us a clear answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, thank you Mr. Hayman. Let us go on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You were asked the following question by Mr. Harmon yesterday, in reference to point 3 of exhibit 86. Exhibit 86 was the signed statement that you signed under duress, you state, concerning the conflict in April: "Question: In your opinion, did the military commanders of the HVO act in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible?" Do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You answered: no. Do you recall your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In giving the answer, can you tell us what HVO commander or commanders do you intend to opine did not act in accordance with international humanitarian standards after exhibit 86 was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who issued orders. I really do not know who issued orders and I cannot tell you which commander. I told you what I had experienced, and which commander issued orders in writing, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your opinion, or do you have an opinion whether Tihomir Blaskic acted in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible as called for in exhibit 86?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, as a doctor, according to the Geneva international conventions, the ill, children, women, should not be mistreated and that is what happened, and pregnant women too. That happened in Vitez and that should not have happened. Who signed the orders I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was: is it your opinion that Tihomir Blaskic failed to act in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible within the meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you have already put that question and you have received an answer. Please go on. You have just asked that question. You wanted to ask the witness regarding point 3, who were the military commanders. Then you went on to say whether Tihomir Blaskic was a member of those commanders. The witness told you that the Geneva Convention envisages that there should be no wounded or killed among old people, women, children et cetera, so proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What he said, your Honour, was: "Who signed the orders I really do not know." That is different from my question. My question is whether he has an opinion whether the accused did or did not act in accordance with this statement. I respectfully think we should get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He told you that he did not know the role of General Blaskic. He told you that, in his opinion, women, children et cetera according to the Geneva Conventions should not be wounded, because in his life he saw that there were wounded. I am sorry for intervening in this way, but I want to make progress. You got your answer; it may not satisfy you but you must go on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will move on, your Honour, but I wish to state my position. He did not answer the question. He gave a non-responsive answer. I have three documents I would like placed before the witness. Doctor, you are being shown three documents marked Defence exhibits 32, 33 and 34. The first, 32, is in the English language. I will simply describe it and this will help you in reviewing it as an order signed by Tihomir Blaskic dated April 18th 1993; the second document is a document in the BSC language, and the third document is an English translation of the second document, that is Defence exhibit 33, which reflects that it is a joint order of Commander Hadzihasanovic as well as Tihomir Blaskic made on April 22nd 1993. I would like to call your attention to a provision in each of the orders and then I will ask you a question about them as a whole. The first document, exhibit D32, states in point 2 that it is commanded to exchange the detained soldiers and the civilians at once. The exhibit which is exhibit 34 provides at the bottom of that order that the appointed members of the Commission are authorised to make all the necessary orders, instructions and tasks in accordance with the agreement signed, referencing the agreement to establish a joint operational centre at the level of the BiH Army Third Corps and of the HVO operative zone, Central Bosnia. My question for you is: prior to your testimony in this case, were you shown any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you answer in the microphone? I do not think the interpretation booth picked it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see this paper before. In April, as President of the War Presidency, I received a paper from international organisations, the UNHCR and UNPROFOR, stating that at the level of the operative zone of Central Bosnia and the Third Corps and it was signed by Lieutenant-colonel or Colonel Tihomir Blaskic and Hadzihasanovic, and on the basis of these orders we proposed to set up three working groups. It is said in this information that a third group was established too, that would be working in the hotel Tisa in Busovaca under the control of European monitors, a joint group at the level of the Third Corps, and the operative zones of Central Bosnia. This paper though I did not see it; I cannot even read it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told before your testimony by representatives of the Prosecution's Office that they were going to ask you in your testimony your opinion whether HVO commanders violated point 3 of exhibit 86? Were you told that in advance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I came here to testify as a doctor and as a person. My wife and my family were against my testifying, but I came here, and I am not involved in politics. I was not involved in politics before and I am not involved in politics now. I made a statement to the investigators of the Hague Tribunal and they invited me -- they asked me whether I would come to tell my story and I did that. I do not know what I could say to you in response to this. I have told you quite simply several times what I did and how I did it. I said that I was informed about the existence of these commissions, that there was a joint commission. I remembered that in this joint commission, Franjo Nakic from Vitez were there too and these others, I do not know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, doctor, and let me be the first to thank you for coming here to provide your testimony to the Tribunal. We are grateful for persons like yourself willing to come and testimony, but my question is a simple one. Before your testimony, did you receive some form of notice, whether through a practice examination or otherwise, that the Prosecutor, Mr. Harmon, was going to ask you to opine whether or not HVO commanders violated point 3 of exhibit 86?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Harmon, Mark Harmon, asked me to tell my story and he told me to tell you the truth and that the truth is the strongest weapon of all and I told you the truth. During these past few days, that is the only thing that Mr. Mark Harmon asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it your testimony you have never had a discussion with Mr. Harmon about what questions he would ask and what your answers would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On what ground, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My objection is: clearly this is an irrelevant area of cross-examination. I have clearly met with this witness and I intend to meet with every other witness. If counsel are suggesting that I have told this witness what to say, I think he should make that complaint in front of your Honours, but I think to air that publicly is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am not making that complaint, your Honour, but the witness has said he did not have a practice exam with Mr. Harmon, and Mr. Harmon has said "Of course he did, all witnesses do and they will", and I accept that representation. What I am trying to get at is: did the Prosecutor's Office know and intend to ask this question and purposefully not show the witness orders of my client going to this very issue, which were in their possession. We got these orders, exhibits D32, 33 and 34, from the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, I wish to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). Mr. Hayman, Mr. Prosecutor, the Trial Chamber has considered this question, that is the investigations done in this case by the Defence as to what may happen between the Prosecutor and the witness. The Tribunal is of the opinion that it should not involve itself with this question. It is the relationship between the Office of the Prosecutor and its witness. As for you, Mr. Hayman, if during your questioning you note that regarding this or that point, the witness was not familiarised with such and such a document, you may do so, but to put the question like a policeman, like an investigating judge, to see what happened within the confidential relationship between the Prosecutor and the witness, that is not appropriate. It would be as if the Prosecutor were to ask you, Mr. Nobilo, or you, Mr. Hayman, when you have a witness, "What exactly happened in your relationship between the witness that you are offering and yourself?" For example, you may draw your own conclusion from the lack of familiarity of this witness with that document, but the Trial Chamber will not involve itself with these matters. We will not repeat this again. So please continue your questioning with the documents that you are producing, and you will see what the witness will tell you. The incident is closed. It is now 1.00. We will resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, Mr. Registrar, will you have the accused brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Mujezinovic, is it correct that you had contact with members of the Vitezovi unit in connection with rendering medical treatment in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did extend medical treatment to Croatian soldiers, HVO and whoever else came among them; the Vitezovi, we extended aid to them.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In connection with that work, would you have conducted medical exams or examinations of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not alone, there were several of us. I said that all the wounded who came were examined, both civilians and military people.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you and your fellow doctors would have conducted those examinations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement that the Vitezovi unit, the members of the Vitezovi unit were on drugs all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you would look at -- if you would retrieve -- and perhaps the usher can assist -- Defence exhibit 31, I would ask that page 3 of that exhibit be put on the ELMO, and the relevant portions to which I will be calling the witness's attention are lines 3 and 4 at the top of the page marked 3 at the bottom of that page. We need the top few lines put on the ELMO, please. Page 3, it is the second page but it is actually numbered page 3, so the back of the first page, at the top of that page. If that could be enlarged, perhaps, and the document moved down a little so it could be even further enlarged. Thank you. I would like to call your attention to a particular sentence. I know this is an English language document so I will read it to you so that it can be properly translated and then I will ask you a question about it. The third full sentence of this page reads as follows and I quote: "The Vitezovi units used to rob apartments and houses and were on drugs all the time." Did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that exactly in the way you have just translated it to me, that it has been translated to me. I told the Hague investigators that units that called themselves HOS and later Vitezovi, that there was a rumour in Vitez that they were on drugs. When I intervened as a doctor to treat Darko Kraljevic, my colleagues Tibold Franjo and Zvonko believed that Darko had a heart attack or had had -- was on drugs. On the way, I heard from them that this was the diagnosis. I did not see those units using drugs, but the story was that they were on drugs and alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The story from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it a remark that was widely spoken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mentioned very frequently, that they were using drugs and they were even trafficking with drugs, particularly among the youth.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On how many --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but I personally did not eye-witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hayman. I wish to consult my colleagues. (Pause). Continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Did you read this statement or rather have it read to you and translated for you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not agree even then, as I said, with the translation. I thought it was not a good translation. I saw not just this but other places that are absurd, and I said that it was not so, but I did sign it in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When it was read to you, did the translator read the acknowledgment at the end of the statement which reads: "This statement has been read to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You knew this statement was to be used potentially in a legal proceeding in which someone could go to jail; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you and I repeat again that I did not agree with the translation which was orally made to me, and what I claimed then and I claim now is that the story was in cafes, in restaurants that this unit was consuming and selling drugs. I had to intervene once as a doctor and two of my colleagues told me: they are on drugs, and you will see what you will do; it is our belief that it is a coronary. I personally never eyewitnessed the taking of drugs or the selling of drugs. I did not sit with them in cafes, I did not socialise with them.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the time you signed the statement, did you tell anyone that you believed portions of it were incorrect or incomplete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I told the investigator of the Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who was that? Do you remember the name of the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The President and the judges are not here to conduct enquiries into the way in which investigations were done. The judges are here to follow the hearings and to rule whether Mr. Blaskic is guilty or not. I think, Mr. Hayman, you have asked a question correctly; the witness answered it. I would like the Prosecutor to make a comment on its investigation, if he will. If not ... Mr. Prosecutor, do you wish to comment, or Mr. Kehoe. It is not an enquiry that the President is doing; it is simply to ask you whether you have any comments to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have previously made an objection about the questions about the manner of the conduct of the investigation. I raised that objection earlier; it was sustained. We are revisiting the issue; I suspect we will continue to revisit that issue. I would object to the continued line of questioning in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just a moment. The issue is whether the witness made this statement in his statement, and to whom he may have made it. I cannot call the investigator to tell the court whether or not the witness made this statement unless I can identify the investigator. It is certainly within my right to call the investigator to impeach the witness if in fact the witness would be impeaching. If this is sensitive information I have no objection to the witness writing this on a piece of paper and submitting it under seal, confidentially into the record. I am not trying to disclose anything confidential, but I think this is a fair question in any system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Prosecutor, that the point made by Mr. Hayman differs a little from the one we had this morning. This morning, we, the judges, intervened because there was something wrong in the way in which the Defence counsel was questioning the witness. However, now we are dealing with something slightly different which can be very important for the Defence; that is to see whether the statement made by the witness that he is coming back to is important or not. As it is important for the Defence, the Tribunal does not wish to make an enquiry within an enquiry; that is not its role, therefore we are going to summarise the situation as follows. The questions put by the Defence are legitimate and it differs from what was said this morning. If the witness wishes anonymously to write on a piece of paper the name, to show his goodwill, he may do so. Generally speaking, the court has heard what has been said, all of it is in the record and the court will come to its own conclusions as to what it should bear in mind of what has been said and what it should not take into consideration. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am very willing to provide to the Defence the name of the investigator or investigators who took this statement. I am not sure the witness remembers. If he does, he can answer; if he does not, I will supply the name of the investigator or investigators who took this statement to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Greg. He is here. I cannot remember the name of the other investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This problem will come up again and the Tribunal has faced it frequently in the past, the question of the statement taken in Serbo-Croatian, then translated into English as a rule, and then when the witness reads it, he is doing so in his own language. The judges have already decided to improve the system of taking of statements with the OTP. For the moment we are going to close this incident. If the witness wishes to answer, and he has already done, he may do so and he need not. What is very important for the Tribunal is that we know which is the final statement, which is the truth for the witness today in answering the questions by Mr. Hayman. I think that is clear, so we can go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Did you ever see a copy of this statement, which is the long ten-page statement, in the Bosnian language, or is the only copy you ever saw the English language copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read a statement in Bosnian, and I said that it was not a good translation, and that there are many discrepancies. It was a very bad translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think this question has already been posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That, your Honour, was with respect to the four-page second statement. I am just trying to find out which statements this witness has seen so we know where the accurate testimony is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw both documents, both this one and the other one. The first was a poor version of the Bosnian. It was in Bosnian, but a poor translation, and orally, when they translated the other one to me, I also said it was a poor version. I know very little English.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just to make it perfectly clear, you saw both of your statements which are Defence exhibit 30, the four-page statement, and Defence exhibit 31, the ten-page statement, in the Bosnian language in print; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not both, only one, only the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say the first, are you referring to the four-page statement or the ten-page statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first ten-page statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Referring, your Honour, to Defence exhibit D31, the ten-page statement. Thank you, doctor. How many times did you treat Darko Kraljevic for a medical problem or administer an injection to him or otherwise see him in a medical capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went only once to treat Kraljevic Darko, I have already answered that question. Do I need to repeat once again the whole story?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I am not asking for a long answer. My question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The treatment lasted ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Over that ten-day period, how many times did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have conversations with him on each of those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already told you that every evening or afternoon, sometimes with his wife, he would come by car. He would drive me to the medical centre. I had to wait in the surgery until the nurse gave him the shot intravenously. After he was administered the injection, he would keep me up to a hour, a hour and a half -- twice his wife was with him -- just to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Darko Kraljevic abuse narcotic drugs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him use drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you conclude as a result of treating him that he had suffered an overdose of cocaine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In my statement I said that the colleagues who came to pick me up to ask me to examine him because they were afraid, they thought it was either a coronary or an overdose. Dr. Franjo Tibold asked me to go to Darko Kraljevic's house and he said to me, "Mujezin, you must go. If you are not willing to go, his soldiers will take you by force." I as a doctor gave him an injection that is given for detoxification after abuse of alcohol and I gave him a diazepam and he felt better and he received those injections over a period of ten days. Anyway, I think you can find all this written down in the medical register.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could the ELMO be turned on, please? I would like to read the next two sentences after following the sentence that I read a moment ago. This is from the second page, although it is marked page 3, of Defence exhibit D31: "On a certain occasion, I managed to bring Kraljevic out of a crisis induced by drugs due to overdosing. I believe it was cocaine." Have you ever made that statement, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not agree with that statement because this is what I said, that there were suspicions that he had an attack induced either by drugs or a heart problem, because there was the story going round Vitez that he was on drugs.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those two sentences I read to you, were they translated to you by the interpreter who read you the statement before you signed it in the same way that they were translated for you today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise, we do not understand, Mr. Hayman. I think the judges and I have told you what is important is the truth, therefore I think the question is very simple. It is no longer a question of finding out whether this statement was made, whether that is in contradiction with what he said today. You can deduce what you like from that, but for the moment I think the problem is a simple one, and I wish to insist that we return to the simplicity of the question. Will you ask the witness whether, yes or no, he administered, after he noted an overdose such as he mentioned in his first statement -- whether he did that or not. He will answer yes or no, and then you will simply deduce from that that the statement differs from what he is saying now. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you manage to bring Kraljevic out of a crisis induced by cocaine due to an overdose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that it was cocaine, because that cannot be established without laboratory tests and you know that very well. In order to prove that, you need special laboratory tests to establish what kind of poison or narcotic drug is in question. I said what I administered. I can only make a temporary diagnosis; whether it is correct or not, that is another matter, it is just the hypothesis. You need objective laboratory tests to prove that diagnosis. In medicine, that is how you proceed, we may assume.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the patient conscious when you saw him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The patient was conscious, he was very disturbed, he was psychotic.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he had ingested or injected any substance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I examined him, I did not ask him anything, I gave him a shot. He was choking, he was very disturbed. I gave him diazepam and an injection for detoxification and he calmed down after five minutes. You can bring over my colleagues who were present who will tell you that he insulted them, saying they did not know anything and that I solved his problem in five minutes, so you see -- how can I answer questions on medicine here?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, if he was not capable of speaking to you, you can simply tell us that and that is fine. I am not asking for anything further in that regard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he was conscious, that he was not in a coma, that he was very aggressive, that he was cursing, that he was walking around, he was insulting people. After the therapy he calmed down in five minutes. I do not know what else I could tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have answered our question. I thank you. Based on your various treatments and encounters with Darko Kraljevic, would you agree with the statement that he was not psychologically stable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he was not a stable person psychologically, that he is emotional, that he tends to overreact, and with such people you cannot foresee what their next reaction will be. That is the way he behaved. In our language, they say he was -- you know, pretending to be very important. He was a show-off, he would fight with people, he always wanted to be at the very top. That is the way he was. People tended to avoid him. He was strong, a big man.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that he was a psychologically unstable person?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, the witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like a direct answer, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He has provided the court with a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Answer briefly, doctor, please, quickly and briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was psychologically unstable, explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have outlined on the transparency that is currently placed on top of Prosecution's exhibit 45 the area belonging to the Kolonija neighbourhood. I call your attention back to it. During the conflict in April 1993 in Vitez, was Darko Kraljevic in control of the part of Vitez called Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned in my statement that he gave me two telephone numbers when I was brought in to work on 19th April. I was told by these people that he had his command in a building -- I can show you which building -- in Kolonija. If you are interested in that, I can show the building to you.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to do that in a moment, but first I would like to ask it again: is it your opinion that during the April conflict in 1993 in Vitez that Darko Kraljevic was in control of the neighbourhood called Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not know that, who exercised control where and who commanded where. I really do not know that, because I had no opportunity of seeing that or finding out.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could assist, your Honour, and place the statement of the witness which is exhibit D30, that is the four-page statement on the ELMO. I am going to have to ask the usher to stand by, because the portion of the statement to which I would like to call the witness's attention begins at the bottom of the page marked 3 and then carries over to the top of the page marked 4. So we are going to read from the bottom of page 3 and the top of page 4 of that statement. If the page could be moved up slightly perhaps it can be enlarged a little bit more. Thank you. Let me read the first two sentences to orient you, doctor. This is the beginning of the paragraph at the bottom: "As I mentioned in my earlier statement, Darko Kraljevic visited me in the War Hospital on April 18th 1993. I did not have any contact with Darko after that." It is this sentence I would like to call your attention to: "However, I know that during the April conflict in Vitez, Darko was in control of the part of Vitez called 'Kolonija' and was headquartered with his soldiers in the building called 'Banjalucanka' marked '4' in the aerial photo." First, do you agree with the statement: "I know that during the April conflict in Vitez Darko was in control of the part of Vitez called 'Kolonija'."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I said that I was taken away on the 19th. Secondly, after that, I really did not see Darko Kraljevic again. Thirdly, this building is across the street from my building and there were soldiers in front of the building and his soldiers had two cafes in the building there. For example on one occasion I went to have a tooth extracted by my colleague, Zoran Markovic, a dentist. I went with Dr. Tibold, and they told me, "These are the soldiers of Darko Kraljevic in the cafes in the same building. They will not do you any harm; do not worry", because I really would not dare walk around. It is true, they confirmed that he was in that building when I went to have a tooth extracted. Rumour also had it that he even had cameras there and that they could follow passers-by and whoever was there. I was taken on 19th April 1993, not the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will bring you the red pen and then perhaps you could mark the building called Banjalucanka on the transparency. Could you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the whole building of Banjalucanka. Cafes were there and here (indicates), and I was not there in the office, but Dr. Markovic and Dr. Tibold told me that Darko was here with his command.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Shall we mark that building with a K for Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear you. I cannot hear an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your question again, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I mark that building, the one you have indicated with a letter K to indicate Kraljevic headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I told you that Dr. Franjo Tibold and Dr. Zoran Markovic showed me where Darko Kraljevic's command was, but I also said that I was never in that building and I never saw Darko Kraljevic sitting there. That is what I told the investigators too, and I was told, "Do not worry." I had a terrible pain in my tooth and Dr. Markovic extracted a tooth of mine that day. I showed you the building, I marked it, and the cafes where I saw soldiers and I was told that they belonged to Darko Kraljevic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it then it is your testimony that the pertinent statement I read beginning on page 3 and carrying over to page 4 of the four-page statement which is exhibit D30 -- your testimony is you never made that statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that I never made that statement; I said that I did not say it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Registrar, everything is in the record, I think, and this is the answer the witness has been trying to give you for many minutes. This must be taken very clearly. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you told us everything you can about what you told the investigators concerning Mr. Kraljevic's control of Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, this is the second time I am telling you this. I did not know who was in command, where. I really did not know. I really did not know that. I did not know. I just told you that Dr. Tibold and Dr. Markovic -- Dr. Zoran Markovic told me that Darko Kraljevic was in that building with his command and we saw soldiers in these cafes that I pointed out to you, and they said, "These are Darko's soldiers." Which part of town was under his command I really do not know. Can you understand me? At that moment, I had been waiting for three days for somebody to kill me and now you are asking me to find things out, to be an investigating judge. what part of town was Darko Kraljevic in charge of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Doctor, you must know that the Tribunal is most appreciative of the effort you are making. The Tribunal is trying to ensure justice and that is our role. I know that all these questions coming to you from the Prosecution and the Defence after many years after those painful events are complex, difficult and painful, but you must at the same time understand the questions put to you by the Defence, because they are defending the interests of General Blaskic. The Tribunal is also here to keep calling to order both the Prosecutor and the Defence. There is a point beyond which we will not tolerate things. Mr. Hayman, when you ask a question, try not to repeat the same question. The witness has told you what he has to say. I will try to synthesise. I think that we have, by now, realised that the witness made these statements, and that today, many months later, he does not find the exact words in those statements. He is not confirming fully what was said there. Put the question to him so that you know exactly what he thinks today, but the Tribunal will not allow two, three, four times the same questions to be put from different angles. Please bear this in mind. We are unanimous in that respect. It is true that you have been doing your cross-examination for longer than you said, and the Tribunal wishes to take this trial forward. Do you need a rest? If you need a rest we are willing to give you a rest so that you can calm down, which seems to be lacking at this point, and the judges wish to restore that serenity to the proceedings. Do you need a rest, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me? No, I would like for us to finish. I do not understand. You see, I am telling you that I cannot claim, nor did I ever claim, because I absolutely could not find out and therefore how could I claim that a man was a commander of Rijeka. How would I know who was the commander? That is what the Defence keeps asking me to do, to say that. General Blaskic did not give me a list of his commanders, saying Darko Kraljevic is in charge of Kolonija and whatever. How should I know? I do not know, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, doctor. The Tribunal is simply saying that there were statements that were made and it is quite normal for the Defence to try and find out which statement precisely reflects your opinion, so tell us what you think today, and you could say that statement corresponded to what you thought at the time or perhaps there were problems of interpretation, so please try and calm down, answer the questions and tell us exactly what you think, and if there is a contradiction between that and your previous statement, you will simply say so. We have wasted five minutes, but the Tribunal felt it necessary to make these remarks. Mr. Hayman, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Doctor, your testimony today: is there any truth or basis in the statement I read to you concerning Kraljevic's control of Kolonija, or do you totally repudiate that statement as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, I am telling you again that I did not agree with the interpretation. Secondly, I did not say that Darko Kraljevic is in command in Kolonija. I am saying that for the third time. I did not say that to anyone. I said that Darko Kraljevic had a command post, as my colleagues told me, in an apartment building there called Banjalucanka. I do not know what else I could tell you, and whether he was commander of all Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibits that have been marked during this testimony are D30, the four-page statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you help me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think the document D30 is the four-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the number on top? It began "Mujezinovic number ..."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me get it. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to have the numbers now. D30 will be exhibit witness statement, the four-page witness statement; is that correct, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: D31 is the same but consisting of ten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then D32 will be the document signed by General Blaskic, is that right, in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: D33 is an exhibit in Serbo-Croatian. Is that this one, in handwriting. So we have these five exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then, your Honour, the transparency, I would like to mark it "Doctor MM" and admit it with the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Why MM, Mr. Hayman? Yes, I understand. What is the number of the transparency?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is an exhibit just like any other. D35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you do not mind, Mr. Hayman, is that acceptable? No objections? Mr. Prosecutor, no objections? Very well, have you finished, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have. Doctor, I would like to thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, you are entitled to redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad, do you have any questions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I should like to have some clarifications from you concerning certain points in your testimony yesterday and today. This morning, in your reply to a question put to you by Defence counsel concerning the position -- can you hear me well, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do I need to begin again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your reply to a question put to you by Defence counsel this morning concerning the hierarchy and the position of Mr. Kordic in relation to Mr. Blaskic, I understood that you said that Mr. Kordic was superior to Mr. Blaskic. This raises a very precise question regarding responsibility in the region of Vitez. Was Kordic responsible for the region of Vitez or not? The question becomes even more important in view of the indictment. In the indictment, there is the name of Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic, and they are classified at two different levels. Mr. Kordic in the indictment is referred to as being in: "The political party, name Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has been Vice-President and member of the Presidency of HZ-HB." Therefore this is a political role. Mr. Blaskic is referred to in the indictment: "He held the rank of colonel and was the Commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone of the HVO." So this is military responsibility. In your reply, do you consider Kordic to have been higher hierarchically superior, who also had command over the region of Vitez? Could you give us this clarification? It could be very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dario Kordic was -- in the hierarchy was in the field of politics the Deputy President of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. That is what I knew to the best of my knowledge, but he also held the rank of colonel; that is to say that he had a dual role. Who was superior to who I really do not know; I just know that he had a political position, a political post, Kordic, but he also had a military rank as well. It is unusual in our part of the world, Herceg-Bosna included, that politicians get military ranks. Really who was superior to who I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were a resident of Vitez, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the general opinion of the inhabitants of Vitez, to whom would they address their grievances or their requests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the region of Vitez --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear the translation. I can hear now, yes. Would you please repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the region of Vitez, to whom would one address oneself if you had requests, complaints, grievances or demands? Would it be to General Blaskic or to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were used to addressing the police concerning questions of crime or a court of justice, I do not know who people addressed then. When the HVO government was established in Vitez, I know that they were addressed to because those people were losing their jobs and they sought help from legal authorities, and I never addressed either Kordic or Blaskic, neither me nor my family; that is to say that there was an administrative centre, the municipal part of the building, and I do not know. Kordic lived in Busovaca and he would come to Vitez only from time to time. I do not know what Kordic was in Busovaca, but I just know that he introduced himself as the Deputy President, the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, and what position he had in Busovaca I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He did not reside in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Also in your testimony yesterday, you spoke several times about attacks against civilians, Muslim civilians of Vitez. You mentioned murders, arrests, cases of confiscation, cases of destruction of banks and shops, the butcher's and others. According to you, was there any selective approach to this destruction of particular classes or particular properties, or was it done at random without any discrimination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could put it in the following way: in Vitez, in this part which is marked as Kolonija by the Defence, there was only one building that was owned by the Bosnian Muslims and everything was destroyed. In Vitez, during the night, prominent Bosniak Muslims were robbed and killed. I mentioned in my statement that in January, in Stare Bila in a village on the main road leading to Vitez, one of the richest businessmen from Vitez was killed, Hasan Skopljak. He was robbed too. Also in the village of Nadioci near Vitez, another businessman was killed. I also mentioned in my statement -- I should not be repeating all of that -- I mentioned quite a few things. We used to have a communist system; we had state firms. For example the firm Krivaja from Sajidovic was destroyed, the commercial bank of Travnik was destroyed. The butchery, it is a chain of stores with their main office in Zenica, all of that was destroyed. I also mentioned that only one establishment, one catering establishment in the neighbourhood of Rijeka in Vitez was owned by a Croat and that was destroyed. All other shops, all other establishments were absolutely under the control of the HVO, the military and the police. Finally, in Vitez, 48 people remained in Vitez of Muslim origin, women, men and children, 5,000 were expelled. Not a single one of these people has returned to that area. In my opinion, this is a well-planned action of ethnic cleansing. I worked as a doctor, specialist, for 22 years, my wife as an economist too, and everything we had was there. People came and took that. I asked a friend of mine, an engineer, Jozo Drovic, "Jozo, what is this?" He said, "This is Croat historical territory." I said, "This is my house." He said, "You made your house there by accident; you lost your way. This is Croat." I cannot understand this as a person. I said, "Jozo, you can call your house whatever you wish, but you cannot call my house that." He said, "No, no, we are rectifying historical mistakes." I do not know if I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You are very clear. I have a further question, a clarification, concerning the Ahmici massacre. You referred to that massacre, and you said that even animals were killed, human beings and animals. What were the dimensions of this massacre? Do you know more or less who were the perpetrators of that massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the village of Ahmici, there is an upper part of this village which is ethnically pure and then there is the lower part. We in Vitez called it Zume. There were mixed houses, Croat houses, Muslim houses. I think there were even Serbs there, because this was owned by the municipality and they gave plots of land to people to build houses. I said in my statement what I was told by two nurses, that at 1.00 am, all the Croats were moved out of Ahmici where there was a mixed neighbourhood so that in the morning at 4.30 am, everything that could move was killed. The upper Ahmici, the upper part of the village Ahmici, was unaffected. I am saying that in November the Croatian Democratic Community in lower Ahmici offered to people to hand over their weapons. They made a list, the HVO soldiers, because the HVO army was of the Croatian Democratic Community. In lower Ahmici, Santic Nenad, an HVO soldier, and a local Muslim collected weapons from the people who had them. They were guaranteed absolute security. Sefkija Djidic reported that all these people reported in Vitez for their work assignments. I asked Nazif Ahmic, an engineer, "Why did you hand over your weapons you had bought primarily from Croats?" He said, "We are in favour of co-existence of peace. We do not want to wage war with the Croats. They are guaranteeing security and safety to us." Your Honour, not a single one of these people survived the massacre in Ahmici, a single one of these people who had surrendered their arms, handed over their weapons. According to the reports I received officially, in Ahmici 118 children, women, were killed. The main point is that the army was not there. These were civilians, primarily. All the houses of the Muslims and the stables and barns were destroyed. It is a village, you know. The two local mosques. I entered Ahmici because they took me there twice a week by car, actually to work as a specialist in Busovaca. I came there after seven days. I could not believe that there were people who could do something like that. I do not know if I have been clear.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you are clear. You could not believe that people could do that, but which people? Could we know whether they were military men or civilians who committed this massacre? Who are the people who collected the arms from the citizens before this massacre was committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Santic Nenad and Ahmic Fahrad, they collected the weapons of the local people. That is what Mr. Sefkija Djidic reported to us and they reported for their work assignments too. Your Honour, I did not see who did that, who had shot these people. I said in my statement that two nurses told me about the events in Ahmici. I came into Ahmici after seven days. I was in an ambulance with a driver called Vujica, I think, who was taking me to work to the neighbouring municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: Doctor, like the President I appreciate that you must feel the way you do, but, like him, I ask you to bear with me. This is a court of law, and we have the responsibilities which you know courts of law have. A moment ago, you told my colleague Judge Riad that the army was not there; you were talking about Ahmici. Just by way of clarification, would I be right in understanding you to mean that the army of the BiH was not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did not mean that? What army were you referring to when you said, "The army was not there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, in the village of Ahmici, there were no soldiers, there were no military formations, no armed formations, there were no army units stationed in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that soldiers were on leave. At that time, soldiers had to leave their weapons in their barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Ahmici, there was no BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand you. May I take you back to that portion of your evidence in which you were talking about allegations to the effect that armed informal gangs might have been committing certain acts. You remember that part of your testimony. I recall also something in what you said to the effect that it would be strange if such armed informal gangs were around with a lot of soldiers under the control of the HVO being also around. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you say that to anyone at the time, that this would be strange, if informal armed gangs were around at the same time when HVO soldiers were present in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, your Honour, some time at the end of April or the beginning of May, Mr. Anto Valenta, one of the Vice-Presidents of Herceg-Bosna, claimed to us at the meeting of the Crisis Staff that the Croat people or the HVO in Vitez is very well armed, 90 per cent of them, he said, and, according to his estimates, only 10 per cent of the Muslims are armed and HOS is a minimal force in Vitez. He claimed that 90 per cent of the HVO army was armed even then, and he asked us not to put up any resistance because we did not stand a chance. I did say in my statement that I said on several occasions at Crisis Staff meetings when Anto Valenta would say -- many times when an excess incident happened, he said, "You know, these are informal groups which are not under our control." That was foolish, in my opinion with such a lot of army and such a lot of police in my opinion, that was part of a plan, an overall plan, because things were done in a planned fashion. You see, in October, I think the beginning of November, they destroyed ten buildings and then they convened a meeting to quiet the situation down. You have a tense situation and in this way they show, "See what can happen if you do not accept this?"

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand this. Do I understand you right to be saying that it was your opinion then that it would be foolish to suggest that armed informal gangs could be in the neighbourhood without the approval of the HVO? Was that your opinion at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My second question is: did you express that opinion in one way or another to anyone in authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that, but I always received the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a subsidiary question. There was a question of armed personnel. I think Mr. Hayman or Mr. Nobilo referred to them as armed people, extraneous to the region, who might have come in on or around the period beginning 15th or 16th April 1993. The question was asked of you as to whether you saw any regimental patches being worn by them. You said, I thought, that you saw some oak leaves. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nodded).

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any or a portion of the insignia to connect them or not to connect them in your mind with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a unit came to Vitez. I do not know where they came from, but they were called -- I am not sure, I think they were called Dominik Pavlovic. People said that they came from western Herzegovina. They came in the first half of January. They created chaos in Vitez, you know, destruction. Whatever little had remained, they had finished off. They broke into people's apartments at night together with HVO soldiers. My opinion is that they were brought to Vitez in accordance with a programme to make chaos, so that they could make people move, because at that time, people were moving out of Vitez. We had refugees who were fleeing from Vitez because they were afraid to remain in Vitez. My wife, my children, I, I knew almost 90 per cent of all the people in the municipality and my wife asked me that we should leave Vitez. She was afraid for the children. You know what, I can claim that not a single Croat doctor helped the population of Vitez, the Croat population of Vitez, as much as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are going into another area, doctor. Let me put it this way to you: some people from outside of the area came into the area in January and created havoc. Was it your appreciation of the situation that what they were doing was known or was not known to the HVO personnel who were in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say what I think, that they were one army, just like the BH-Army was one army. They had their command, they had their chain of command, their hierarchy, and a military formation cannot just enter a town and do whatever they wanted to do. In my opinion, you know, I had done my military service in the army and for a soldier to do what he was doing, he had to have orders, and I think that this unit received orders and some of the local people from the HVO were with them, not all of them but some.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a connected question. Did you see any of the local HVO people trying to stop this outside unit from doing what it was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, the policy was as follows: who is against this is against us. I mentioned the example that Croats were beaten up in Vitez and I can say that not very many people can dare say that they were beaten up and I can also claim the following: when I worked from 19th April 1993 in the health centre, a lot of Croats came to see me as a doctor and they would put into my pocket 100 or 150 Deutschemark and they would say, "It is very difficult for you Muslims so keep this", but they do not dare say that now because they will be beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us go back to the remark which you made a while ago about your own stint of military service. I think you gave about a year's service towards the end of your medical training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So you would have had some exposure to military organisational matters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not have the transcript before me, so if I am in error, do correct me. Am I right in recalling that you described General Blaskic as Commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I repeated twice that I personally never met Mr. Blaskic. I saw his signatures, and I was told -- it is a small town, you know. In Vitez, Filip Filipovic was the Commander of the HVO. I was told Mr. Blaskic had come to Vitez in, I think, the second half of 1992, I do not know exactly. I never talked to Blaskic. I did not. I know the man from pictures and from the street. It was said that he was the Commander of the HVO. Only later in the autumn it was said that an operational zone of Central Bosnia was formed and that Mr. Blaskic, who was a lieutenant colonel, became the Commander of the operational zone of Central Bosnia, I think some time in the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman introduced in evidence a document which you saw, I believe, D32. It is signed by the accused as "Colonel Blaskic" and it is dated, I think, 18th April 1993. Did you see the document? Would you like to see it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will just read it as an introduction to what I really want to ask you. It begins this way: "On the basis of the orders given by the HVO Head of Staff, HZ Herceg-Bosna, office number 02 2/101 G48/93, dated April 18th, in order to obey it completely, I command ...", and then there is a series of items setting forth specific orders. Did you see that document in which he says, "I command ..." and signed it as Colonel Blaskic. Am I right in my recollection that you saw on the television statements to the effect that corrective action would be taken by Mr. Blaskic in relation to various outrages which were being committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time at the beginning of November at a meeting, I mentioned in my statement that the representatives of the HVO, the Croatian government in Vitez, told us that the Commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia, Mr. Blaskic, would prevent through his orders looting and robbery and that he would not allow weapons to be taken from BH-Army soldiers and that BH-Army convoys can freely pass through, provided they are announced. I said there and then and I still believe that this document -- I said ten minutes ago that after these orders issued by Mr. Blaskic -- I do not know how big his influence is in the army, but if somebody is signed "Commander" in an army, then people are supposed to obey him. After that, 5,000 Muslims were expelled from Vitez. I do not know whether Mr. Blaskic had the power and strength to prevent that. I do not know. I really do not know what the military hierarchy was in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: did you become aware of any public statement denying that General or Colonel Blaskic had the necessary authority to issue orders with a view to preventing those things from happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the course of your evidence, under cross-examination by Mr. Hayman, you spoke on the question of control over Kolonija. You did so specifically in relation to a gentleman by the name of Darko Kraljevic. Am I pronouncing it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You also outlined Kolonija with the assistance of Mr. Hayman on the transparency which is on the easel. Kolonija as you outlined it includes the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you happen to know where Colonel Blaskic resided at the time, that is during the period beginning 15th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 15th April 1993. Your Honour, Mr. Blaskic is well known in Vitez as Commander. When he came first of all he fortified in a military sense the hotel Vitez. What I encircled is the urban area of Vitez and that is where he commanded his army from. I went to see Mario Cerkez in Kolonija; he was also commander of a unit. You know, an army cannot have only one unit. I know --

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To be brief, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to this, it would seem that Darko Kraljevic was the Commander of Commanders in my opinion. I am not an expert in hierarchy in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My question was a simple one. It was whether Kolonija, as you outlined it, included the hotel Vitez and whether Colonel Blaskic resided at the hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that, I did not see that. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR.. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In response to Mr. Hayman, you said that "General Blaskic did not give me a list of his commanders." Should I understand you to mean that in your mind General Blaskic had the authority to issue such a list, the problem being that you did not have that list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If the Commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia signs a document as Commander, he has to know who is under his command in Central Bosnia and which units are under his command. It is only a normal sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, the Tribunal wishes to thank you. It is aware of the effort that this entailed for you, and the suffering that it must have entailed to relive through all those experiences. I will not put to you any further questions. I should simply like you to know that, appearing before this International Criminal Tribunal, you should have the feeling that you have said everything that you have to say about the totality of the grave crimes of which General Blaskic is accused, so I am not asking you a question, I simply wish to ask you whether you have a declaration to make or any additional points to make. If not, you can go back home, and I hope you will find there all the serenity that you crave. Is there something that you have not told us or questions that you would like to raise that were not put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, gentlemen from the Prosecution and the Defence, I have come here as an individual to give you my story, as Mark Harmon has said, and nothing more than that. I shall be happy and satisfied if this lofty Tribunal achieves the prevention of such crimes anywhere in the world again and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar and Mr. Usher, will you accompany the witness and after that, the Trial Chamber will rise until 4.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, Mr. Registrar, please bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel, good afternoon. The Prosecutor with your permission, Mr. President, would like to call Mr. Lars Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, your Honour, may I just advise the court that we were handed a minute or two ago a document entitled "War Diary from Bosnia" which states: "This diary is an edited version of the battle field diary which I kept during my service as an ECMM monitor." The name Lars Baggesen appears under it. I do not know where this came from, if it has been in the possession of the Prosecution or if the witness mailed it in, but it is some 33 single-spaced pages in length. I am sure there will be no cross-examination this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Hayman. First of all, we too have a letter from Mr.s Vidovic, I think. It is a different document. There are many different documents. Mr. Hayman, first, let us go in order. Where did you receive this document from?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
