utterances.text: The Registrar, the court Registrar was kind enough to hand it to myself and Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Nobilo's is in Croatian, mine is in English. We are grateful for that fact, but I wish to advise the court we will be studying this as quickly as we possibly can, but, of course, for the time being we must listen to the witness and his testimony. I do not know if we have any other objection to make until we have a chance to read it tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where does this document come from, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a war diary kept by the witness who is about to appear in front of you. It was served on the Defence in its original language, which was Danish, in September last year. It remained in the Danish language, this is my understanding, for a considerable period of time, I believe, and it may have been the Defence requested that it be translated into the Croatian language, and that was done. The Prosecutor did not do anything with this document. Eventually, and this is a very short period of time ago, certainly to my knowledge within the last two to three weeks, an English translation from the Croatian version was produced. The document that has just been handed to Mr. Hayman is a corrected version of that English translation, so in that sense, it is new to us as well, but it is in essence an English translation of an original Danish document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Still we have a paradoxical situation, that an exchange of documents is being made before any decision has been taken by the Tribunal on the submission of evidence and regarding the witnesses too, so now the Defence has a document which needs to be communicated to the Prosecution which has just been translated into English. Is that so, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Actually, almost so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, we will take note of it. We will not delay the debate any further, and we are going to bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a minute please. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you please tell the judges and me your full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, my full name is Lars Borhoj Baggesen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Baggesen. Will you now read the solemn statement which has been given to you. It is actually an oath. LARS BORHOJ BAGGESEN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baggesen. Please take a seat. You have been brought before the Trial Chamber I within the framework of the charges brought against Colonel Blaskic. You are a witness of the Prosecution, who will first question you and then you will be cross-examined by Defence counsel. Mr. Prosecutor, how much time have you planned for this examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would estimate five hours for the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Baggesen, could you please tell the court the nature of your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an officer in the Danish Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What rank are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A major.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year did you join the Danish Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the army in 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were in the home guard whilst you were at high school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then you went into the regular army after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it correct that from 1976 to 1977, you attended the Danish Army combat school at Oxbolt in Denmark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This was a course to train junior officers for the Danish Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the nature of the training that you underwent at Oxbolt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically we were trained in infantry and armoured tactics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This school trained only combat officers for the Danish Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By "combat officers", what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means we were trained to command the units in battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What year were you commissioned into the Danish Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you joined the Danish Royal Hussars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What type of regiment is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a cavalry regiment and now it is an armoured regiment with tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So originally a horse-mounted regiment, now an armoured regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was your first job with the Royal Hussars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first job in the first two years was to train the new professional soldiers. During that period I had another job, because this was only a peacetime job. My wartime job was as an intelligence officer at the 2 Zeeland Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In Denmark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As an intelligence officer, what sort of work were you involved with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were making analysis of the Soviet Bloc and the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This was at a time when there was a confrontation between NATO during the Cold War and the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have formal training as an intelligence officer in the Danish Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had training at the army special school in intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying you have a trained eye for military intelligence matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What rank were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was second lieutenant and then I was promoted to lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1986 I think you commanded a reconnaissance platoon of the Royal Danish Hussars. Can you explain to the court the role of a reconnaissance platoon in the Danish Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This reconnaissance platoon, we were trained to find the enemy's frontline, to fight on the enemy frontline, and do reconnaissance behind the enemy frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A certain intelligence role in that job as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you had a break from your regiment in 1981 and performed some United Nations service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the court about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was ordered to Cyprus where the United Nations had forces, and I had a job as air liaison officer at the Danish headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were also involved in training Danish soldiers in Cyprus, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my job was to co-ordinate all the helicopter flights in that area and I had to train all the Danish soldiers to work with the helicopters and do some airborne training.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think from the wings on your chest you are also an airborne-trained Danish officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1986 to 1990, I think you were the Operations Officer for Home Guard Region 5 and the second in command of Home Guard District 92, based in Roskil in Zeeland in Denmark; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What rank were you at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I think I was first lieutenant and later on promoted to captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What job did this involve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My job as operations officer, I was responsible for the planning of the operations and trained the units to carry out those operations, and as the job as second in command, I was the person who was to take over if the commander was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Or indeed if the commanding officer was killed you would take over, as second in command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what the Danish Home Guard constitutes, what is it made up of in Denmark? What is its role in Danish national defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Danish Home Guard is a volunteer force who are a part of the Danish armed forces and it consists today -- I think we are 60,000 people, all civilians who are training during weekends and holidays to do this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So your soldiers are part-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are not professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But the commanding officer and a number of his staff are regular soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, officers from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From 1990 to 1995, I think you worked for the Danish Chief of the Defence Staff, the most senior officer of the Danish Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is commanding the Danish armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it was during this period that you volunteered for service as a monitor with the European Community Monitoring Mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will come back to that, but if we just move forward to your present day job, I think in 1995 you were promoted to major; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were then given command of your own Home Guard district, District 53 based at Ringsted Barracks in Denmark; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What are you now responsible for as commanding officer for of that unit? How many men do you command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the command of 1,600 men and women and they are organised in 17 companies. I have one headquarter company, two police companies, one special reconnaissance company; the rest of them are infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So the district is subdivided into companies, those are the smaller units under your command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are going to be using this terminology quite a lot in the course of your testimony, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you have two police companies under your command. That is not unusual for you, coming from Denmark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think lastly, you teach and train intelligence officers of the Danish Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think after you returned to Denmark from your service in the former Yugoslavia, you indeed trained future monitors for the ECMM mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were also requested last year by the Danish Centre for Human Rights to train civilian human rights monitors for service in Ceczna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that you have been a cavalry officer in the Danish Army for over 20 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Serving both with the Danish Army and the European forces of NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How familiar would you say you are with armoured and infantry tactics and training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think after all those years I am very familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you are probably also quite familiar with the amour and infantry training and tactics of the Soviet Bloc, what was the Soviet Bloc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are you also familiar with the term FIBUA or fighting in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what that is, whether or not it is actually a recognised military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually fighting in built-up areas is a very difficult operation to carry out, therefore normally military units try to avoid going into built-up areas, because it is difficult to fight in built-up areas, not only because of all the buildings but there are a lot of civilians in that area. Therefore normally armies try to avoid going into built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I can take you back a couple of years, this is the material part of your testimony; you have given your background now. When I ask you questions, can you address your answers to the judges rather than to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that in 1992, the Danish Government issued a general request for volunteers from the armed forces for service in the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you volunteered for service, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For which months and of which year did you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I volunteered in 1993 and I did service down there for the end of March and April, May and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I realise these events are from some years ago, and this is not a memory test, but I do understand that you kept a diary of events, a personal diary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that diary with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to use it to refresh your memory and refresh your memory only if you need to when you are answering questions either from the Prosecutor or the Defence. If you wish to take it out you may now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what the ECMM was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ECMM was a monitoring mission established after there was made a memorandum of understanding in 1991 and the purpose was this, monitoring mission was to monitor the withdrawal of the forces after the first cease-fire in the first fightings down in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe it was the creation of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe which was held at Brindisi in 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you have said, its purpose was to monitor the withdrawal of the JNA and its heavy weapons back to barracks after events in Slovenia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But that role changed, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because when the tension started in Bosnia, it was agreed to send the monitoring mission down to Bosnia to monitor the situation in that area. At that time, that was before the United Nations Protection Forces went to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What specifically was the role of the ECMM in, now, Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our role was to liaise with the civilian and the military authorities in that area, trying to make cease-fire in that area and trying to establish peace again in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you wore a distinctive uniform, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you please translate ECMM for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. ECMM stands for European Community Monitoring Mission. Is that correct, Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I asked you whether or not you wore a distinctive uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were dressed in white so it was easy for the parties down there to recognise us and we were wearing a blue cap and we were wearing the EC symbols on our shoulders. We were unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that you arrived in Zagreb on 30th March 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you were given a briefing of the position on the ground in Central Bosnia, the disposition of military forces, the relevant authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally when new monitors arrived to the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb, we all had a briefing on what was happening down there. We had a briefing on the different forces in that area, and we had a briefing on how to use communication equipment we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where were you going to be stationed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first day after we arrived to Zagreb, we were told that I, together with two other Danish monitors, were going to Zenica to the Regional Centre in Zenica, whose area of responsibility was the central part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you told who the relative factions, the relevant factions were in that area of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that the two factions down there were the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you told about their military forces; were they identified to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told about HVO and BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which were which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO were the Bosnian Croats and BiH were the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were you told about levels of armament, how well equipped the two forces were, how well organised they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told during the briefing in Zagreb that HVO forces were better equipped than BiH and we were told that they had more weapons and more men than BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would like to show you a diagram, Major Baggesen, which you in fact produced for me which I think will explain to the court the structure of the ECMM and where the Vares parts of it were stationed. If the witness could be shown this? (Handed). Major Baggesen, if you would place that on the ELMO next to you? Mr. Registrar, what is the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, could you explain to the court what this structural diagram represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. We had the headquarters of the ECMM, situated in Zagreb. The headquarters commanded a lot of regional centres covering the whole area of the former Yugoslavia, and I will now tell about the Regional Centre at Zenica where I was ordered to. The Regional Centre was divided in three co-ordination centres and at the Regional Centre in Zenica there were three monitored teams who reported directly to the headquarters, the Regional Centre in Zenica. One team called Zulu 1 had an area of responsibility in Zepce, another team, Zulu 2 had an area of responsibility in Vares, and Zulu 3 in Kakanj. Then the Regional Centre had a European Community liaison officer to the UNPROFOR forces in Kiseljak. This liaison officer was the link between UNPROFOR and ECMM in Central Bosnia. Then the Regional Centre commanded three co-ordination centres and each of those co-ordination centres had two or three monitored teams who had each their own area of responsibility. All these teams from the co-ordination centres were reporting daily to the co-ordination centre. The co-ordination centre made a summary of what had happened in that area and reported to the Regional Centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was very similar to a military command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and one of the reasons is because all the monitors were experienced officers, so even though it was a civil organisation, it was manned by officers from the EC countries and from some of the ECLO countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In which of the teams did you serve in your three months in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served in the teams Zulu 1, Zulu 2, Zulu 3 and V1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you were responsible for Zepce, Vares, Kakanj and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Over a three-month period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Not all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If there is no objection from the Defence, Mr. President, I would like exhibit 87 admitted into evidence, please. Am I correct in saying, Major Baggesen that you arrived in Zenica on 2nd April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: At that time, the Regional Centre in Zenica was headed by a professional diplomat from France, Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were the Deputy Head and the Operations Officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Deputy Head was Juan Valentin, who was a Spanish monitor and the Operations Officer was Dimitrios Dagos who was a Greek officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is a map next to you. I wonder if the camera can be brought in on it. I just would like you to show where Zenica is in relation to various other towns in Central Bosnia, just so we can all become acquainted with the area in which you were serving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zenica is situated here (indicates) in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where is Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kiseljak is south of Zenica, between Zenica and Sarajevo, down here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just put your pointer on Sarajevo. Can you just identify the municipalities of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Busovaca is situated here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you also identify the municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Travnik is here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you take a seat, please, Major Baggesen. Am I right in saying that the three teams that operated from Zenica, which was Zulu 1, Zulu 2 and Zulu 3, operated in all those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zenica, did you receive a further briefing from that which you had received in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had a briefing on what was happening in the central part of Bosnia. We had a briefing on the two parties in that area. We were briefed on who was the Commander of the HVO and who was commanding BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were you told was commanding the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that General Hadzihasanovic was commanding the Third Corps of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By BiH you mean the Bosnian government forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who were you told was commanding the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you meet both of these gentlemen while you were serving in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you meet General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact numbers, but I think 10 or 15 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you meet Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the same, 10 or 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you look around the court and see if you can see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, General Blaskic is sitting over there (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the areas for which these commanders were responsible identified to you by monitors in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during a briefing we were told mostly on what area they were covering with the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you stand up and identify on the opstina map of Bosnia firstly the area for which General Hadzihasanovic, you believe, was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We believe he was responsible for the BH forces in Zenica, in Travnik, part of Vitez, Kakanj, and Zepce, Zavidovici, Mr.konjic and some of the forces in south of -- there down in Gornji Vakuf, Fojnica and Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now can you identify on the same map and also recite the municipalities for the transcript, the municipalities for which General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of Zenica, Travnik, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Busovaca, Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak, Visoko, Kakanj and Gornji Valuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, if you would take a seat. That information was based on information that had been gathered over a number of months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During your time in Bosnia, do you believe that to be correct from your experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the ECMM also chaired an organisation called the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what was the Busovaca Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Busovaca Joint Commission was a commission made in the beginning of 1993. It was situated in the village called Busovaca; that is why it was named the Busovaca Joint Commission. Later on, before I arrived, the Busovaca Joint Commission was moved from Busovaca to an ECMM-rented house in Vitez, close to a British UNPROFOR battalion. This commission was manned by representatives from HVO and from BiH and from ECMM. When I arrived, there were three members from HVO representatives. The representatives were Mr. Franjo Nakic, who we were told was the deputy to Colonel Blaskic and two other senior officers. The senior representative from BiH were Mr. Merdan, who we were told was the deputy to General Hadzihasanovic from the Third Corps, and there was two senior officers from BiH as well. We were three ECMM monitors and one ECMM monitor who was chairing the Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the function of the Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The function was to get the two parts to co-operate and try to solve problems in this Commission, and we normally had a meeting every morning where we were sitting around a green table and discussing what has happened the last 24 hours. After discussing what had happened the last 24 hours. We divided into a number of teams consisting of one representative from BiH --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could stop there a moment, Major Baggesen. Can the witness be shown exhibit 80(6). I have it if you have to scrabble through a thousand documents down there. This is a photograph that has been previously admitted into evidence. If it could be placed on the ELMO? (Handed). Do you recognise any of the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Colonel Blaskic and I recognise Franjo Nakic who is sitting beside him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Again I repeat the question: who was Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Deputy of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is how he represented himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were moving on to explain the function of the Busovaca Joint Commission. If you could explain to the court what sort of day-to-day work you were dealing with. One point: was the Busovaca Joint Commission the creation of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an agreement between all three parties to have this Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know when it was created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So if you could explain to the court what your day-to-day business was concerned with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our day-to-day business was that we had this meeting early in the morning where we discussed the incidents that happened the last 24 hours, and sometimes one party would have some complaint on what the other parties had done and we would discuss these things. There were a lot of rumours we had to investigate, and normally after we had a meeting, maybe one hour, we would divide it in three teams, each team with one ECMM monitor, one representative from HVO and one representative from BiH, and then we went out to investigate that specific area, to see what had happened, and we used a lot of time just investigating rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it was to build trust between the parties and try and maintain some sort of peace in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that you travelled out with the parties. Were you able to freely travel anywhere you wanted with the representatives of the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally we were, but it was sometimes difficult because there were a lot of checkpoints in the area and sometimes when we were going to a specific area where we were told something had happened, sometimes we went into a checkpoint where we were not allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you get around that problem of getting through checkpoints that you were not allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Often we had to return to Vitez, at the hotel Vitez, where Colonel Blaskic had his headquarters, and representatives of HVO had to see him to get a written order so we could pass the checkpoint and have access to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the representative of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That depends on who was with that team, but even if it was Mr. Nakic it was not enough. We often had to have a written order from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of these written orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember I saw one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing by whom it was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Blaskic's signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you had these orders, did you have any problems getting through the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did the same apply to get through Bosnian army checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that we had problems in that area. We had a problem later on, but that was in the northern part of -- north of Zenica, not in that area down there where the Busovaca Joint Commission operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in the Central Bosnia region you had no problem travelling through Bosnian army checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Major Baggesen, I would like to move on now to the subject of military communications. Do you know who controlled the telephone lines in the central Bosnian region. When I ask that, you can identify the municipalities, if you know the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the answer of a part of your question. I know that BiH controlled the PTT lines in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt; by PTT, you are referring to the telephone company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In what was the former Yugoslavia. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew that BiH were in control of the PTT in Zenica, and we knew that HVO were in control of the PTT lines in Vitez, Travnik and Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found out because several times we were not able to have a contact on our landline from our rented house in Vitez, and I was told by one of our interpreters that it was a normal procedure when there were no English-speaking operators at the PTT house in Vitez the line was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By landline, you have just used another military term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The telephone line. Why was it necessary for there to be English-speaking operators at the telephone company in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obvious, because they were able to listen to our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This was told to you by one of your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Croat interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you take any action after you were told this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We already had taken action, because we were not allowed to speak classified on the telephone, but after this, we were more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the Zenica area, I think you have said that the Bosnian government actually controlled the telephone lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have any problems communicating within the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not inside Zenica but we were normally not able to call outside Zenica. We could sometimes but the normal picture was that we were not able to phone out of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the telephone line between Zenica and the other areas were closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We supposed it was HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you travelled to a lot of Bosnian army and HVO military headquarters in your time in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you make observations about the military communications equipment that were in those headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did and we were especially aware because they told us that they did not have any radio equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both sides, so therefore every time when we visited a military headquarters we used our eyes to see if there were any evidence that there were communication equipment in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Specifically talking about HVO headquarters, what communications equipment, apart from telephones, did you observe in those headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At some headquarters we saw telefax machines. At some headquarters we were able to see some radio equipment, and I cannot remember, we saw radio equipment in a few of the headquarters, but in some of the other headquarters we saw antennas. When we could see those antennas we could conclude there was some radio equipment in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have already said that both sides were not open about their communications equipment which maybe is understandable for military forces. The HVO, did they conceal from you the fact that they had communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they tried to hide it from us. Actually, that is very normal for a military unit to show what kind of equipment they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To show or not to show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Specifically talking about the hotel Vitez in Vitez, how many times did you visit that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact numbers, but several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are aware where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see an antenna on that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw antennas in that area. I did not see directly radio equipment, but one day I had a visit there, I was looking through an open door and inside a room and I saw a man with a microphone and I think he was speaking in the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As a professional soldier, what was your impression of what you saw of the HVO communications network?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my opinion, after my experience, I think that you have radio equipment so you are able to command the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you have any examples of the communications network actually working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once I visit a war headquarters, HVO war headquarters, close to a Bosnian Serb Army front who was operated. That was north of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did that indicate to you that the communications network was working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was able to see this operator who was operating the radio equipment and I was able to listen that he had conversation with several other radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have any examples of your visit being known about before you arrived in an area by virtue of radio communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, normally when we came to an area, especially where we had to go back to Vitez to pick up a written order from Colonel Blaskic and when we arrived to the specific area where we are -- the first time we were not allowed to pass the checkpoint. After passing the checkpoint with this written order, it seems like the people we were going to meet were warned about our visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the only manner in which these people could have been warned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By telephone or by radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, it is 5.30. I am happy to continue. It is as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we are going to rise now until tomorrow morning at 10.00. I wish to draw attention, Mr. Cayley, that you are going rather fast and I am afraid that the interpreters are having a little difficulty following, so if you could go a little slower tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

procedural_notes.text: (Court adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
